chapters.arabic_text:
### | والمتواطئة والتباس إحداهما بالأخرى

فإن المشتركة في الإسم هي المختلفان في المعنى المتفقان في الإسم، حيث لا
يكونبينهما إتفاق وتشابه في المعنى البتة، وتقابلها المتواطئة وهي
المشتركان في الحد والرسم المتساويان فيه بحيث لا يكون الإسم لأحدهما بمعنى
إلا وهو للآخر بذلك المعنى، فلا يتفاوتان بالأولى والأحرى والتقدم والتأخر
والشدة والضعف كإسم الإنسان لزيد وعمرو، وإسم الحيوان للفرس والثور؛ وربما
يدل إسم واحد على شيئين بمعنى واحد في نفسه، ولكن يختلف ذلك المعنى بينهما
من جهة أخرى ولنسميه إسما مشككا، وقد لا يكون المعنى واحدا ولكن يكون
بينهما مشابهة ولنسمه متشابها.
أما الأول فالكالوجود للموجودات؛ فإنه معنى واحد في الحقيقة ولكن يختلف
بالإضافة إلى المسميات، فإنه للجوهر قبل ما هو للعرض ولبعض الأعراض قبله
لبعض آخر، فهذا بالتقدم والتأخر. وأما المقول بالأولى والأحرى فالكالوجود
أيضا فإنه لبعض الأشياء من ذاته ولبعضها من غره، وما له الوجود من ذاته
أولى وأحرى بالإسم، واما المقول بالشدة والضعف فيتصور فيما يقبل الشدة
والضعف كالبياض للعاج والثلج، فإنه لا يقال عليهما بالتواطؤ المطلق
المتساوي بل أحدهما أشد فيه من الآخر.
أما الحيوان لزيد وعمرو، والفرس والثور فلا يتطرق إليه شيء من هذا
التفاوت بحال، فقد ظهر بهذا الفرق انه قسم آخر، والمشكك قد يكون مطلقا كما
سبق، وقد يكون بحسب النسبة إلى مبدأ واحد كقولنا طبي للكتاب والمبضع
والدواء، أو لانتسابه إلى غاية واحدة كقولنا صحي للدواء والرياضة والفصد.
وقد يكون إلى مبدأ وغاية واحدة كقولنا لجميع الأشياء أنها الإلهية. وأما
الذي لا يجمعهما معنى واحد، ولكن بينهما تشابه ما كالإنسان على صورة متشكلة
من الطين بصورة الإنسان وعلى الإنسان الحقيقي، فليس هذا بالتواطؤ إذ يخلفان
بالحد فحد هذا حيوان ناطق مائت، وحد ذلك شكل صناعي يحاكي به صورة حيوان
ناطق مائت؛ وكذلك القائمة للحيوان وللسرير حده في أحدهما أنه عضو طبيعي
يقوم عليه الحيوان ويمشي به، وفي الآخر أنه جسم صناعي مسدير في أسفل السرير
ليقله ولكن نجد بينهما شبها في شكل أو حال. ومثل هذا الإسم يكون موضوعا في
أحدهما وضعا متقدما ويكون منقولا إلى الآخر، فإن أضيف إليهما  سمي متشابه
الإسم، وإن أضيف إلى المتقدم منهما سمي موضوعا، وإن أضيف إلى الأخير سمي
منقولا؛ ثم هذا الضرب من التشابه على ثلاثة أقسام: الأول أن يكون في صفة
قارة ذاتية كصورة الإنسان. والثاني أن يكون في صفة إضافية غير ذاتية كإسم
المبدأ لطرف الخط والعلة.
والثالث أن يكون التشابه جاريا في أمر بعيد كالكلب لنجم مخصوص ولحيوان،
إذ لا تشابه بينهما إلا في أمر بعيد مستعار لأن النجم رئي كالتابع للصورة
التي كالإنسان، ثم وجد الكلب أتبع الحيوانات للإنسان فسمي باسمه. ومثل هذا
ينبغي أن يلحق بالمشترك المحض، فإنه لا عبرة بمثل هذا الإشتباه فقد صارت
الأسامي بهذه القسمة ستة: متباينة، ومترادفة، ومتواطئة، ومشتركة، ومشككة،
ومتشابهة؛ لأن العقل إذا قسم الشيء إلى ستة أقسام فيحتاج إلى ست عبارات في
التفهيم.

### | إرشاد إلى مزلة قدم المتباينات

ولا يخفى أن الموضوعات إذ تباينت مع تباين الحدود فالأسامي متباينة
متزايلة كالفرس والحجر، ولكن قد يتحد الموضوع ويتعدد الإسم بحسب اختلاف
إعتبارات، فيظن أنها مترادفة ولا تكون كذلك؛ فمن ذلك أن يكون أحد الإسمين
له من حيث موضوعه، والآخر من حيث له وصفن كقولنا سيف وصارم؛ فإن الصارم دل
على موضوع موصوف بصفة الحدة بخلاف السيف، ومن ذلك أن يدل كل واحد على وصف
للموضوع الواحد كالصارم والمهند، فإن
أحدهما يدل على حدته والآخر على نسبته، ومن ذلك أن يكون أحدهما بسبب وصف،
والآخر بسبب وصف الوصف كالناطق والفصيح. ومن المتباينة المشتق والمنسوب مع
المشتق منه والمنسوب إليه كالنحو والنحوي، والحديد والحداد، والمال
والمتمول، والعدل والعادل، فإن العادل لو سمي عدلا كما سميت العدالة عدلا
كان ذلك من قبيل ما يقال باشتباه افسم، ولكن غيرت الصيغة وبقيت المادة
والمعنى الأول زيد فيه ما دل على زيادة المعنى فسمي مشتقا.

### | القسمة السابعة للف المطلق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ط-أ (wa-ṭa-ʾa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "treading" or "leveling" — a path that is beaten down and thus equally traversable by all; hence, equality and uniformity of application.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In logical/theological usage, denotes a term applied to multiple subjects with perfect equality of meaning, without priority (taqaddum) or intensity (shiddah) — the opposite of ambiguous (mushtarak) and analogical (mushakkik) predication.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of "level ground" metaphorically extended to conceptual equality; the rhetorical contrast is with tashkīk (gradation), where the literal sense is retained but with relational variance.
- Root: ش-ك-ك (sh-k-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes doubt or piercing; in this context, the term "penetrates" multiple subjects with one meaning but with varying degrees of intensity or priority.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for a predicate applied to multiple subjects with a single meaning but differing in priority (al-awlawiyyah), precedence (al-taqaddum), or intensity (al-shiddah) — e.g., existence (wujūd) applied to substance before accident.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz (metaphorical) usage is excluded here; this is ḥaqīqah with relational gradation, not equivocation.
- Root: ش-ب-ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance or similarity in form or attribute, not identity of essence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, distinguishes metaphorical transfer (naql) from true univocity; resemblance-based naming (tasmiyah bi al-shabah) is a distinct category from both mutawāṭiʾah and mushtarak.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Rhetorical device of istiʿārah (borrowed similarity) — the basis for transferred names (manqūl).
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqābul (Contrastive Pairing) — When two terms are defined by mutual opposition (e.g., mushtarak vs. mutawāṭiʾah), their syntactic and semantic boundaries must be strictly delineated to prevent category confusion (iltibās); this governs the division of terms into six exhaustive categories.
chapters.translation:
---

### On Univocal Terms (al-Mutawāṭiʾah) and the Confusion of One with Another

Know that the ambiguous term (al-mushtarak) is [applied to] two things differing in meaning but agreeing in name, where there is no agreement or resemblance between them in meaning whatsoever. Its opposite is the univocal term (al-mutawāṭiʾah), which is [applied to] two things agreeing in definition (ḥadd) and description (rasm), being equal therein, such that the name is not applied to one of them with a meaning except that it is applied to the other with that very same meaning. Thus they do not differ in priority (al-awlā) or worthiness (al-aḥrā), nor in precedence (al-taqaddum) or posteriority (al-taʾakhkhur), nor in intensity (al-shiddah) or weakness (al-ḍaʿf) — like the name "human" (insān) for Zayd and ʿAmr, and the name "animal" (ḥayawān) for the horse and the bull.

Sometimes a single name indicates two things with one meaning in itself, but that meaning differs between them from another aspect — let us call this the "gradated term" (al-mushakkik). And sometimes the meaning is not one, but there is between them a resemblance — let us call this the "assimilated term" (al-mutashābih).

As for the first [i.e., the gradated term with precedence], it is like "existence" (al-wujūd) applied to existents; for it is a single meaning in reality, but it differs in relation to the named things — for it applies to substance (jawhar) before it applies to accident (ʿaraḍ), and to some accidents before others. This is [gradation] by precedence and posteriority. As for that which is predicated by priority and worthiness (al-awlā wa al-aḥrā), it is also like "existence"; for it applies to some things from their own essence (min dhātihi) and to others from something else (min ghayrihi). That which has existence from its own essence is more worthy and more prior for the name. As for that which is predicated by intensity and weakness, it is conceivable in what admits intensity and weakness — like "whiteness" (al-bayāḍ) applied to ivory and snow; for it is not said of them with absolute equal univocity, but rather one of them is more intense in it than the other.

As for "animal" applied to Zayd and ʿAmr, and to the horse and the bull, none of this variance applies to it in any way. It has thus become clear by this distinction that it is another division [i.e., the univocal]. The gradated term may be absolute (muṭlaq) as previously mentioned, or it may be by relation to a single principle (mabdaʾ wāḥid) — like our saying "medical" (ṭibbī) for the book, the scalpel, and the medicine — or by its relation to a single end (ghāyah wāḥidah) — like our saying "healthful" (ṣiḥḥī) for the medicine, the exercise, and the bloodletting. And it may be [by relation] to a single principle and a single end together — like our saying of all things that they are "divine" (ilāhiyyah).

As for that which is not united by a single meaning, but between which there is some resemblance — like "human" applied to a figure formed from clay resembling the human form, and to the true human — this is not univocal, for they differ in definition. The definition of the one is "a rational mortal animal" (ḥayawān nāṭiq māʾit), and the definition of the other is "an artificial shape by which the form of a rational mortal animal is imitated." Likewise, "standing" (al-qāʾimah) applied to the animal and to the bed — its definition for the one is "a natural organ upon which the animal stands and with which it walks," and for the other it is "an artificial body placed at the bottom of the bed to support it." But we find between them a resemblance in shape or state. Such a name is posited for one of them with a primary positing (waḍʿ mutaqaddim) and is transferred (manqūl) to the other. If it is attributed to both, it is called "assimilated in name" (mutashābih al-ism); if attributed to the prior of the two, it is called "posited" (mawḍūʿ); and if attributed to the latter, it is called "transferred" (manqūl).

Then this kind of resemblance is of three divisions:
- The first: that it be in a settled essential attribute (ṣifah qārrah dhātiyyah) — like the human form.
- The second: that it be in a relational, non-essential attribute (ṣifah iḍāfiyyah ghayr dhātiyyah) — like the name "principle" (mabdaʾ) for the endpoint of a line and for the cause.
- The third: that the resemblance runs in a remote matter (amr baʿīd) — like "dog" (kalb) for a particular star and for the animal; for there is no resemblance between them except in a remote, borrowed matter, because the star was seen as following the figure that is like the human, and then the dog was found to be the most following of animals to the human, so it was named by its name.

Such [remote resemblance] ought to be annexed to the purely ambiguous (al-mushtarak al-maḥḍ), for no heed is paid to such a confusion. By this division, the names have become six: distinct (mutabāyinah), synonymous (mutarādifah), univocal (mutawāṭiʾah), ambiguous (mushtarakah), gradated (mushakkikah), and assimilated (mutashābihah) — because when the intellect divides a thing into six divisions, it needs six expressions for comprehension.

---

### Guidance Concerning the Slipping of the Foot Regarding Distinct Terms (al-Mutabāyināt)

It is not hidden that when the subjects (mawḍūʿāt) are distinct along with the distinctness of their definitions, the names are distinct and mutually exclusive (mutabāyinah mutazāyilah) — like "horse" and "stone." But sometimes the subject is one while the name multiplies according to differing considerations (iʿtibārāt), so one might suppose they are synonymous (mutarādifah) when they are not so.

Among this [is the case] that one of the two names indicates [the subject] by virtue of its being a subject, and the other by virtue of its having a description — like our saying "sword" (sayf) and "sharp" (ṣārim); for "sharp" indicates a subject described with the attribute of sharpness, unlike "sword." And among this [is the case] that each one indicates a description of the single subject — like "sharp" (ṣārim) and "Indian-forged" (muhannad); for one indicates its sharpness and the other its [geographical] relation. And among this [is the case] that one is due to a description, and the other due to a description of the description — like "rational" (nāṭiq) and "eloquent" (faṣīḥ).

And among the distinct [terms] are the derived (mushtaqq) and the relative (mansūb) with that from which they are derived and to which they are related — like "grammar" (al-naḥw) and "grammarian" (al-naḥwī), "iron" (al-ḥadīd) and "blacksmith" (al-ḥaddād), "wealth" (al-māl) and "wealthy" (al-mutamawwil), "justice" (al-ʿadl) and "just" (al-ʿādil). For if the just man were called "justice" (ʿadl) just as justice itself is called "justice," that would be of the kind said by confusion of names (ishtibāh al-ism). But the form (ṣīghah) was changed while the material (mādda) remained, and the first meaning had added to it what indicates the increase of meaning — so it was called "derived" (mushtaqq).

---

### The Seventh Division of the Absolute Term (al-Muṭlaq)

chapters.arabic_text:
### | بالإشتراك على مختلفات

إعلم أن اللفظ المطلق على معان مختلفة ثلاثة أقسام: مستعارة ومنقولة
ومخصوصة باسم باسم المشترك.
أما المستعارة فهي أن يكون إسم دالا على ذات الشيء بالوضع ودائما  من أول
الوضع إلى الآن، ولكن يلقب به في بعض الأحوال لا على الدوام شيء آخر
لمناسبته للأول على وجه من وجوه المناسبات، من غير أن يجعل ذاتيا للثاني
وثابتا عليه ومنقولا إليه
كلفظ الأم، فإنه موضوع للوالدة ويستعار للأرض يقال إنها أم البشر، بل
ينقل إلى العناصر الأربعة فتسمى أمهات على معنى أنها أصول. والأم أيضا أصل
للولد فهذه المعاني التي استعير لها لفظ الأم لها أسماء خاصة بها.
وإنما تسمى بهذه الأسامي في بعض الأحوال على طريق الإستعارة، وخصص باسم
المستعار لأن العارية لاتدوم وهذا أيضا يستعار في بعض الأحوال.
وأما المنقول فهو أن ينقل الإسم عن موضوعه إلى معنى آخر ويجعل إسما له
ثابتا دائما، ويستعمل أيضا في الأول فيصير مشتركا بينهما كإسم الصلاة والحج
ولفظ الكافر والفاسق، وهذا يفارق المستعار بأنه صار ثابتا في المنقول إليه
دائما ويفارق المخصوص باسم المشترك بأن المشترك هو الذي وضع بالوضع الأول
مشتركا للمعنيين لا على أنه استحقه أحد المسميين، ثم نقل عنه إلى غيره إذ
ليس لشيء من ينبوع الماء والدينار وقرص الشمس والعضو الباصر سبق إلى
استحقاق إسم العين، بل وضع للكل وضعا متساويا بخلاف المستعار والمنقول.
والمستعار ينبغي أن يجتنب في البراهين دون المواعظ والخطابيات والشعر، بل
هي أبلغ باستعماله فيها. وأما المنقول فيستعمل في العلوم كلها لمسيس الحاجة
إليها إذ واضع اللغة لما لم يتحقق عنده جميع المعاني لم يفردها بالأسامي،
فاضطر غيره إلى النقل. فالجوهر وضعه واضع اللغة لحجر يعرفه الصيرفي
والمتكلم نقله إلى معنى حصله في نفسه، وهو أحد أقسام الموجودات وهذا مما
يكثر إستعماله في العلوم والصناعات.
وأما المشتركة فلا يؤتى بها في البراهين خاصة ولا في الخطابيات إلا إذا
كانت معها قرينة،
وهي أيضا أقسام: فمنها ما يقع في أحوال الصيغة كالإسم الذي يتحد فيه بناء
الفاعل والمفعول نحو المختار فإنك تقول زيد مختار والعلم مختار، وأحدهما
بمعنى الفاعل، والآخر بمعنى المفعول وكالمضطر وأشباهه. ومنها ما يقع على
عدة أمور متشابهو في  الظاهر مختلفة في الحقيقة لا يكاد يوقف على وجه
مخالفتها كالحي الذي يطلق على الله وعلى الإنسان وعلى النبات والنور الذي
يطلق على المدرك بالبصر المضاد للظلام، وعلى العقل الهادي إلى غوامض
الأمور.
فإن قال قائل: فما مثال المستعار؟ قلنا: مثاله استعارة أطراف الحيوان
لغير الحيوان كقولهم: رأس المال، وجه النهار، عين الماء، حاجب الشمس، أنف
الجبل، ريق المزن، يد الدهر، جناح الطريق، كبد السماء، وكقولهم: بيه سمع
الأرض وبصرها، وكقولهم: أيد للشر ناجذيه، ودارت رحى الحرب، وشابت مفارق
الجبال، وكقولهم: الشيب عنوان الموت، والرشوة رشا الحاجة، العيال سوس
المال، الوحدة قبر الحي، الإرجاف زند الفتنة، الشمس قطيفة مباحة للمساحين.
ومن إستعارات القرآن: (وأنه في أم الكتاب لتنذر به أم القرى ومن حولها)
(واخفض لهما جناح الذل من الرحمة) (والصبح إذا تنفس)) (فأذاقها الله لباس
الجوع والخوف) (كلما أوقدوا نارا للحرب أطفأها الله) (أحاط بهم سرادقها)
(فما بكت عليهم السماء والأرض) (واشتعل الرأس شيبا) (فصب عليهم ربك سوط
عذاب) (ولما سكت عن موسى الغضب) ونظائره مما يكثر، وهذه الإستعارات بنوع
مناسبة بين المستعار والمستعار منه،
فإن قيل: فما معنى المجاز؟ قلنا قد يراد به المستعار فالمعنى أنه قد تجوز
عن وضعه، وقد يراد به ما يقتضي الحقيقة، وفي الإطلاق خلافه كقوله: (وأسأل
القرية) إذ المسؤول بالحقيقة أهل القرية لا نفس القرية؛ فهذه أمور لفظية من
أهملها ولم يحكمها في مبدأ نظره كثر غلطه ولم يدر من أين أتى.

### | الفن الثاني

### | في مفردات المعاني الموجودة

### | ونسبة بعضها إلى بعض

والفرق بين هذا الفن والذي قبله أن الأول نظر في اللفظ من حيث يدل على
المعاني - وهذا نظر في المعنى من حيث هو ثابت في نفسه، وإن كان يدل عليه
باللفظ إذ لا يمكن تعريف المعاني إلا بذكر الألفاظ.
ويتضح الغرض من هذا الفن بأنواع من القسمة.

### | القسمة الأولى في نسبة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ر ك (sh-r-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Partnership, sharing; al-mushtarak is that which is shared among multiple parties without priority of one over another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In logic and theology, denotes a single term applied equally to multiple meanings by original convention (waḍʿ), not by transfer or metaphor.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in its equal application to all denoted meanings; no metaphorical priority.
- Root: ن ق ل (n-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To transfer, move from one place to another; naql in terminology is the transference of a word from its original sense to a new fixed sense.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical transference (manqūl) occurs when the language-maker lacked a term for a novel meaning, so later users transferred an existing term permanently.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Differs from metaphor (mustaʿār) in permanence; differs from homonym (mushtarak) in that it has a historical priority of one sense over another.
- Root: ع و ر (ʿ-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Defect, blemish; ʿārah is a loaned object returned after use.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Metaphor (mustaʿār) is a loaned name, temporary by nature, not constitutive of the thing's essence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Purely figurative (majāz); its use in demonstrative proof is to be avoided, though it excels in oratory and poetry.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Nominal Predication and Syntactic Context (al-ʿamal fī al-ism wa al-khabar): The grammatical form (ṣīghah) may be shared between agent and patient (e.g., mukhtār), requiring contextual disambiguation (qarīnah) to determine syntactic and semantic role.
chapters.translation:
### | On Homonymous Terms Applied to Diverse Meanings

Know that an utterance applied absolutely to diverse meanings is of three divisions: the metaphorical (mustaʿārah), the transferred (manqūlah), and that which is specially designated by the name "homonym" (mushtarak).

As for the metaphorical (mustaʿārah): it is that a name signifies the essence of a thing by original convention (waḍʿ), continuously from the first convention until now, but is applied as a designation in some circumstances—not perpetually—to another thing, due to its suitability to the first in some respect of suitability, without making it essential to the second, nor fixed upon it, nor transferred to it. Like the word "mother" (umm), for it is conventionally established for the parent, yet is borrowed for the earth—it is said she is the mother of humankind. Indeed, it is even transferred to the four elements, and they are called "mothers" (ummahāt) in the sense that they are origins (uṣūl). And the mother is also an origin for the child. So these meanings for which the word "mother" is borrowed have their own specific names. They are only called by these names in some circumstances by way of metaphor (istiʿārah). And it is specially designated as "borrowed" (mustaʿār) because a loan (ʿāriyah) does not endure, and this too is borrowed only in some circumstances.

As for the transferred (manqūl): it is that the name is transferred from its original subject to another meaning, and is made a name for it, fixed and perpetual. It is also used in the first [sense], and so becomes homonymous between the two—like the name "prayer" (ṣalāh) and "pilgrimage" (ḥajj), and the words "unbeliever" (kāfir) and "sinner" (fāsiq). This differs from the metaphorical (mustaʿār) in that it has become fixed in that to which it is transferred, perpetually. And it differs from that which is specially designated as homonym (mushtarak) in that the homonym is that which was established by the first convention as shared equally between the two meanings—not that one of the two named things had priority in deserving it, then it was transferred from it to another. For none of the spring of water, the dinar, the disk of the sun, or the seeing organ has priority in deserving the name "eye" (ʿayn); rather, it was established for all of them with equal standing—unlike the metaphorical and the transferred.

The metaphorical (mustaʿār) ought to be avoided in demonstrative proofs (barāhīn), but not in exhortations, rhetorical discourses, and poetry—indeed, it is more forceful in employing it therein. As for the transferred (manqūl), it is used in all the sciences due to the pressing need for it, since the language-maker, not having ascertained all meanings, did not assign them distinct names, so others were compelled to transfer. Thus "substance" (jawhar)—the language-maker established it for a stone known to the assayer, and the theologian (mutakallim) transferred it to a meaning he obtained in himself, namely one of the divisions of existents. And this is something frequently used in the sciences and crafts.

As for homonyms (mushtarakah), they are not employed in demonstrative proofs specifically, nor in rhetorical discourses, except when accompanied by a contextual indicator (qarīnah). They too have divisions: among them is that which occurs in the forms of the expression (ṣīghah), like the noun in which the construction of the active participle and the passive participle are unified—such as "chosen" (mukhtār), for you say "Zayd is chosen" (mukhtār) and "knowledge is chosen" (mukhtār), one being in the sense of the agent (fāʿil) and the other in the sense of the patient (mafʿūl)—and like "compelled" (muḍṭarr) and its analogues. Among them is that which applies to several things similar in appearance but different in reality, whose point of difference is scarcely apprehended—like "living" (ḥayy), which is applied to God, to man, and to the plant; and like "light" (nūr), which is applied to that perceived by sight, opposed to darkness, and to the intellect guiding to the subtleties of things.

If someone says: "What then is an example of the metaphorical (mustaʿār)?" We say: its example is the borrowing of the limbs of animals for non-animals, like their saying: "the head of wealth" (raʾs al-māl), "the face of the day" (wajh al-nahār), "the eye of water" (ʿayn al-māʾ), "the eyebrow of the sun" (ḥājib al-shams), "the nose of the mountain" (anf al-jabal), "the saliva of the rain-cloud" (rīq al-muzn), "the hand of time" (yad al-dahr), "the wing of the road" (janāḥ al-ṭarīq), "the liver of the sky" (kabad al-samāʾ); and like their saying: "the earth's ear and eye" (samʿ al-arḍ wa baṣaruhā); and like their saying: "he bared his molars at evil" (abdā ʿan nawājidhihi), "the millstone of war turned" (dārat raḥā al-ḥarb), "the partings of the mountains grew white" (shābat mafāriq al-jibāl); and like their saying: "gray hair is the title of death" (al-shayb ʿunwān al-mawt), "bribery is the watering of need" (al-rashwah rashā al-ḥājah), "dependents are the moth of wealth" (al-ʿiyāl sūs al-māl), "solitude is the grave of the living" (al-waḥdah qabr al-ḥayy), "rumor-mongering is the fire-stick of sedition" (al-irjāf zind al-fitnah), "the sun is a spread garment freely given to the destitute" (al-shams qaṭīfah mubāḥah lil-masāḥīn).

And among the borrowings (istiʿārāt) of the Qur'an: {«وَأَنَّهُ فِي أُمِّ الْكِتَابِ لِتُنذِرَ بِهِ أُمَّ الْقُرَىٰ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا»} (And it is in the Mother of the Book; that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it), {«وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ»} (And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy), {«وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ»} (And the dawn when it breathes), {«فَأَذَاقَهَا اللَّهُ لِبَاسَ الْجُوعِ وَالْخَوْفِ»} (So God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear), {«كُلَّمَا أَوْقَدُوا نَارًا لِّلْحَرْبِ أَطْفَأَهَا اللَّهُ»} (Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it), {«أَحَاطَ بِهِمْ سُرَادِقُهَا»} (Its pavilion encompasses them), {«فَمَا بَكَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّمَاءُ وَالْأَرْضُ»} (So the heaven and earth wept not for them), {«وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا»} (And the head blazed with gray hair), {«فَصَبَّ عَلَيْهِمْ رَبُّكَ سَوْطَ عَذَابٍ»} (So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment), {«وَلَمَّا سَكَتَ عَن مُّوسَى الْغَضَبُ»} (And when the anger subsided from Moses)—and their analogues, which are numerous. And these borrowings are by a kind of suitability (munāsabah) between the borrowed and that from which it is borrowed.

If it is said: "What then is the meaning of metaphor (majāz)?" We say: it may be intended to mean the borrowed (mustaʿār), so the meaning is that it has departed (tajāwaza) from its original convention; and it may be intended to mean that which requires the reality (ḥaqīqah), and in its unrestricted application there is its opposite—like His saying: {«وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ»} (And ask the village), for the one asked in reality is the people of the village, not the village itself. These are verbal matters; whoever neglects them and does not master them at the outset of his inquiry, his error multiplies, and he does not know whence it came.

### | The Second Art

### | On the Simple Meanings of Existents

### | And the Relation of Some to Others

The difference between this art and the preceding one is that the first considered the utterance insofar as it indicates meanings—and this considers the meaning insofar as it is fixed in itself, even though it is indicated by the utterance, since meanings cannot be defined except by mentioning utterances.

The purpose of this art is clarified by several types of division.

### | The First Division: On Relation (Nisbah)

chapters.title_en: The Division of Existing Things According to Our Perception, Relative Universality/Particularity, and Individual Entities
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الموجودات إلى مدراكنا

فليعلم أن نظرنا في حصر الموجودات وحقائقها وهي منقسمة إلى محسوسة وإلى
معلومة بالإستدلال لا تباشر ذاته بشيء  من لاحواس، فالمحسوسات هي المدركات
بالحواس لخمس كالألوان، ويتبعها معرفة الشكال والمقادير وذلك بحاسة البصر،
وكالأصوات بالسمع، وكالطعوم
بالذوق، والروائح بالشم، والخشونة والملاسة، واللين والصلابة، والبرودة
والحرارة، والرطوبة واليبوسة بحاسة اللمس، فهذه الأمور ولواحقها تباشر
بالحس أي تتعلق بها القوة المدركة من الحواس في ذاتها. ومنها ما يعلم وجوده
ويستدل عليه بآثاره ولا تدركه الحواس الخمس: السمع والبصر والشم والذوق
واللمس، ولا تناله. ومثاله هذه الحواس نفسها فإن معنى أي واحدة منها هي
القوة المدركة، والقوة المدركة لا تحس بحاسة من الحواس، ولا يدركها الخيال
أيضا.
وكذلك القدرة والعلم والإردادة بل الخوف والخجل والعشق والغضب، وسائر هذه
الصفات نعرفها من غيرنا معرفة يقينية بنوع من الإستدلال لا بتعلق شيء من
حواسنا بها. فمن كتب بين أيدينا عرفنا قطعا قدرته وعلمه بنوع من الكتابة
وإرادته إستدلالا بفعله، ويقيننا الحاصل بوجود هذه المعاني كيقيننا الحاصل
بحركات يده المحسوسة وانتظام سواد الحروف على البياض، إن كان هذا مبصرا
وتلك المعاني غير مبصرة بل أكثر الموجودات معلوم بالإستدلال عليها بآثارها
ولا تحس، فلا ينبغي أن يعظم عندك الإحساس وتظن أن العلم المحقق هو الإحساس
والتخيل وأن ما لا يتخيل لا حقيقة له، فإنك لو طالبت نفسك بالنظر إلى ذات
القدرة والعلم وجدت الخيال يتصرف فيه بتشكيل وتلوين وتقدير، وأنت تعلم أن
تصرف الخيال خطأ وأن حقيقة القدرة المستدل عليها بالفعل أمر مقدس عن الشكل
واللون والتحيز والقدر، ولا ينبغي أن تنك دلالة العقل على أمور يأباها
الخيال.
وننبهك الآن على منشأ هذا الإلتباس؛ فتأمل أن المدركات الأول للإنسان في
مبدأ فطرته حواسه فكانت مستولية عليه،
ثم الأغلب من جملتها الأبصار الذي يدرك الألوان بالقصد الأول والأشكال
على سبيل الإستتباع، ثم الخيال يتصرف في المحسوسات وأكثر تصرفه في المبصرات
فيركب من المرئيات أشكالا مختلفة آحادها مرئية، والتركيب من جهته، فإنك
تقدر أن تتخيل فرسا له راس إنسان وطائرا له رأس فرس، ولكن لا يمكن أن تصور
آحادا سوى ما شاهدته البتة حتى أنك لو أردت  أن تتخيل فاكهة لم تشاهد لها
نظيرا لم تقدر عليه، وإنما غايتك أن تأخذ شيئا مما شاهدته فتغير لونه مثلا
كتفاحة سوداء، فإنك قد رأيت شكل التفاحة والسواد فركبتهما أو ثمرة كبيرة
مثل بطيخة، فلا تزال تركب من آحاد ما شاهدت لأن الخيال يتبع الإبصار ولكنه
يقدر على التركيب والتفصيل فقط، ولا يزال الخيال متحركا في التركيب
والتفصيل مستوليا عليك بذلكن فمهما حصل لك معلوم بالإستدلال انبعث الخيال
محدقا نظره نحوه طالبا حقيقة الأشياء عنده، ولا حقيقة عنده إلا للون أو
الشكل فيطلب الشكل واللون، وهو ما يدركه البصر من الموجودات حتى لو تأملت
في ذات الرائحة تأملا خياليا طلب الخيال للرائحة ولونا ووضعا وقدرا، كاذبا
فيه وجاريا على مقتضى جبلته.
والعجب أنك إذ تأملت في شكل متلون لم يطلب الخيال منه طعمه ورائحته وهما
حظا الشم والذوق، وإذا تأملت في ذات الطعم والرائحة طلب الخيال حظ البصر
وهو اللون والشكل، مع أن الخيال يتصرف في مدركات الحواس الخمس جميعا ولكن
لما كان ألفه لمدركات البصر أشد وأكثر، صار طلبه لحظ البصر أغلب وأبلغ.
فإذا عرضت على نفسك عملك بصانع العالم وأنه موجود لا في جهة، طلب الخيال له
لونا وقدر له قربا وبعدا واتصالا بالعالم وانفصالا إلى غير ذلك مما شاهده
في الأشكال المتلونة، ولم يطلب له طعما ورائحة. ولا فرق بين الطعم والرائحة
واللون والشكل، فالكل من مدركات الحواس. فإذا عرفت إنقسام الموجودات
إلى محسوسات وإلى معلومات بالعقل ولا تباشر بالحس والخيال، فاعرض عن
الخيال رأسا وعول على مقتضى العقل فيه، فقد ظهر لك إنقسام الموجود إلى
محسوس وغيره.
؟؟؟

### | القسمة الثانية للموجودات باعتبار نسبه

؟؟؟ بعضها إلى بعض بالعموم والخصوص
إعلم أن معنى من المعاني الموجودة، وحقيقة من الحقائق الثابتة إذا نسبتها
إلى غيرها من تلك المعاني والحقائق، وجدتها بالإضافة إليه إما أعم وإما أخص
وإما مساويا، وإما أعم من وجه وأخص من وجه، فإنك إذا أضفت الإنسان إلى
الحيوان وجدته أخص منه، وإن أضفت الحيوان إلى الإنسان وجدته  أعم منه، وإن
أضفت الحيوان إلى الحساس وجدته مساويا له لا أعم ولا أخص، وإن نسبت الأبيض
إلى الحيوان وجدته أعم من وجه فإنه يشمل الجص والكافور وجملة من الجمادات،
وأخص من وجه فإنه يقصر عن تناول الغراب والزنوج وجملة من الحيوانات.
فإذن جملة الحقائق تناسبها بهذا الإعتبار لا تعدو هذه الوجوه الأربعة،
فقس على ما ذكرناه ما لم نذكره.

### | القسمة الثالثة للموجودات تنقسم إلى

### | موجودات شخصية معينة وتسمى أعيانا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-س-س (ḥ-s-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sensory perception; the five external senses as instruments of direct apprehension.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥiss denotes the faculty of immediate perception, contrasted with ʿaql (intellect) which grasps non-sensible realities.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for direct sensory contact; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to intellectual "perception."
- Root: د-ل-ل (d-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Indication, sign, or evidence leading to knowledge of what is hidden.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Istidlāl is rational inference from effects (āthār) to causes or unseen realities—a central epistemic method in kalām.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical pointers; metaphorical for intellectual proof.
- Root: خ-ي-ل (kh-y-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Imagination; the faculty that composes and decomposes sensory images.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Khayāl is the internal sense that retains and recombines forms but cannot originate novel simples—only recombine perceived ones.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for mental imagery; metaphorical for false supposition.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqdīr (Ellipsis/Suppletion) — In phrases like "فليعلم أن نظرنا في حصر الموجودات" the implied subject is the reader's intellect; the imperative "فليعلم" governs a nominal clause with an understood "أنت" (you), requiring the reader to supply the omitted agent for proper parsing.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that our inquiry into the enumeration of existing things and their realities divides them into two classes: those perceived by the senses (maḥsūsāt) and those known by inference (maʿlūmāt bil-istidlāl) whose very essence no sense directly apprehends. The sensibles are what the five senses perceive—such as colors, and following upon them the knowledge of shapes and magnitudes, all by the sense of sight; sounds by hearing; tastes by the tongue; odors by smell; and roughness, smoothness, softness, hardness, cold, heat, moisture, and dryness by the sense of touch. These matters and their concomitants are directly contacted by sense, i.e., the perceiving faculty among the senses attaches to them in their very selves.

Among existing things, however, are those whose existence is known and inferred from their effects (āthār), yet the five senses—hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch—neither perceive them nor reach them. An example is these very senses themselves: for the meaning of each one of them is the perceiving power (al-quwwah al-mudrikah), and the perceiving power is not sensed by any of the senses, nor does imagination (al-khayāl) grasp it either.

Likewise, power (al-qudrah), knowledge (al-ʿilm), will (al-irādah)—indeed, fear, shame, love, anger, and all such attributes—we come to know them in others with certain knowledge by a kind of inference, not by any of our senses attaching to them. Thus, when someone writes before us, we know with certainty his power and knowledge by the very act of writing, and his will by inference from his deed. Our certainty of the existence of these meanings is like our certainty of the observed movements of his hand and the orderly arrangement of black letters upon white—if that is visible—while those meanings are not visible. Indeed, most existing things are known by inference from their effects and are not sensed. Therefore, you should not magnify sensation in your estimation, nor suppose that verified knowledge is sensation and imagination, and that whatever is not imaginable has no reality. For if you demanded of yourself to contemplate the very essence of power and knowledge, you would find imagination (al-khayāl) busying itself with them by giving them shape, color, and measure—while you know that imagination's operation is erroneous, and that the reality of power, inferred from its act, is sanctified above shape, color, spatial occupation, and quantity. It is not fitting that you reject the intellect's indications concerning matters that imagination refuses.

Now I alert you to the source of this confusion. Consider that the first perceptions of a human being at the beginning of his natural constitution are his senses, which thus dominate him. Then the most prevalent among them is sight, which perceives colors as its primary object and shapes secondarily. Then imagination operates upon the sensibles—most of its operation being upon visible things—composing from visible objects various forms whose individual components are seen, while the composition is from its own doing. For you can imagine a horse with a human head, or a bird with a horse's head; but you cannot picture any individual component other than what you have actually witnessed, ever. Even if you wished to imagine a fruit you had never seen the like of, you could not; your utmost is to take something you have seen and alter its color, for instance, like a black apple—for you have seen the apple's shape and blackness, so you combine them—or a large fruit like a watermelon. Thus you keep composing from the individual components of what you have witnessed, because imagination follows sight, yet it is capable only of composition and decomposition. Imagination never ceases moving in composition and decomposition, dominating you thereby. So whenever something known by inference comes to you, imagination rushes forth, directing its gaze toward it, seeking the reality of things within itself—and in itself there is no reality except color or shape. So it seeks shape and color, which is what sight perceives of existing things. Even if you contemplated the very essence of an odor with an imaginative contemplation, imagination would seek for the odor a color, a position, and a quantity—lying therein and following the dictate of its own nature.

And it is strange that when you contemplate a colored shape, imagination does not seek from it its taste and odor—which are the shares of smell and taste—whereas when you contemplate the essence of taste and odor, imagination seeks the share of sight, namely color and shape. This is so even though imagination operates upon the perceptions of all five senses; but since its familiarity with the perceptions of sight is stronger and more frequent, its seeking the share of sight becomes more prevalent and more forceful.

So when you present to yourself your inference about the Maker of the world—that He exists, not in a direction—imagination seeks for Him a color, and assigns Him nearness and distance, connection to the world and separation from it, and other such things witnessed in colored shapes; yet it does not seek for Him a taste or an odor. And there is no difference between taste, odor, color, and shape—all are among the perceptions of the senses. Since you now know the division of existing things into sensibles and things known by the intellect that are not directly contacted by sense or imagination, turn away from imagination entirely and rely upon the dictate of the intellect in this matter. For the division of the existent into the sensible and the non-sensible has become clear to you.

### | The Second Division of Existing Things, According to Their Relation to One Another by Universality and Particularity

Know that any meaning among existing meanings, or any reality among established realities, when you relate it to others of those meanings and realities, you find it in relation to that other either more general (aʿamm), or more specific (akhaṣṣ), or equal (musāwin), or more general in one respect and more specific in another. For if you relate "human" (al-insān) to "animal" (al-ḥayawān), you find it more specific than it; if you relate "animal" to "human," you find it more general. If you relate "animal" to "sentient" (al-ḥassās), you find it equal to it—neither more general nor more specific. And if you relate "white" (al-abyaḍ) to "animal," you find it more general in one respect, for it includes plaster, camphor, and a host of inanimate things; and more specific in another respect, for it falls short of covering the crow, black people, and a host of animals. Thus, the totality of realities, in this respect, does not exceed these four modes. So measure by what we have mentioned whatever we have not mentioned.

### | The Third Division of Existing Things: They Divide into Individual, Particular Entities, Called "Aʿyān" (Essences/Individuals)
