The knowledge of these parts is prior. Then if these too are known by definition, a knowledge of the parts of their definitions must precede them — and so on to infinity. But it terminates at conceptions that are primary, known by observation through an inner or outer sense without definition, and upon them it stops.

Likewise, assent to the conclusion necessarily requires the prior knowledge of the premises, and so too the premises until one ascends to primary truths whose assent is obtained not by demonstration. So their saying remains: "How were those primary truths present in us while we are unaware of them, or how did they arise after not being, without acquisition, and when did they arise?"

We say: Those sciences are not actually present in us at every moment. But when the natural disposition of the intellect is completed, those sciences are in us potentially, not actually. Its meaning is that we have a power that apprehends the universal simples with the aid of the outer and inner sense, and a reflective power (quwwah mufakkirah) that arises for the soul whose function is composition and analysis, able to relate the simples to one another. And we have a power that apprehends what the reflective power has effected of the relation between the simples — namely, the relation between them by negation and affirmation. So it apprehends the eternal and the originated and relates one to the other. The rational power then precedes to the judgment of negation — namely, that the eternal is not originated — and relates "animal" to "human" and judges that the relation between them is affirmation — namely, that the human is an animal.

This power apprehends some of these relations without a middle term, and does not apprehend others, so it halts in need of a middle — as it apprehends "world" and "originated" and the relation between them, but does not judge negation as it judged between the eternal and the originated, nor affirmation as it judged in the case of animal and human. Rather, it halts to seek a middle — namely, to know that the world does not depart from originated things and thus does not precede them, and that whatever does not precede originated things is originated.

If it is said: "You have divided these assents into what is known by a middle and what is known primarily without a middle. But these assents are necessarily preceded by conceptions, for one does not know that the world is originated unless he knows 'originated' as a simple and 'world' as a simple; and one does not know 'originated' unless he knows an existence preceded by non-existence; and one does not know existence preceded by non-existence unless he knows non-existence, existence, priority, and posteriority — and that the priority here is of non-existence and the posteriority of existence. These simples must be known. But if their apprehender is sense, then sense apprehends only a single particular — so assent should be only in a single particular. Thus when one sees a particular person and that his whole is greater than his part, he should not judge that every whole is greater than its part, for he has observed by sense only a specific person. Let him judge concerning that specific person and suspend judgment concerning other persons until observation. But if he judges universally that every whole is greater than its part, whence does he get this judgment, since his sense apprehended only a particular person?"

We say: The universals are intelligible, not sensible; and the particulars are sensible, not intelligible. The universal judgments belong to the intellect upon the universal intelligibles. This is disclosed by the distinction between the intelligible and the sensible. For "human" is intelligible, and it is sensible as observed in a particular person such as Zayd. By its being apprehended in two ways, we mean that the sensible human cannot be sensed except conjoined with a specific color, a specific quantity, a specific position, and a specific proximity or distance. These are accidental things accompanying humanity, not essential to it — for were they to change, the human would still be that human. As for the intelligible human, it is "human" only, shared equally by the tall and the short, the near and the far, the black and the white, the smaller and the larger, with one single sharing. So you have a power that presents "human" conjoined with matters foreign to humanity, and it cannot present it except conjoined with these foreign matters — that power is called sense and imagination (khayāl). And you have another power that presents "human" stripped of the foreign matters, and were their opposites supposed, they would not affect it — that power is called the rational power. So it has become clear to you that between the sense's apprehension of the specific person encompassed by foreign accidents not entering into his quiddity, and the intellect's apprehension of the bare quiddity of the thing not conjoined with what is foreign to it, there is the utmost distance. And the universal judgments are upon the universal quiddity stripped of matters and foreign accidents.

If it is said: "How does a universal knowledge arise from observing a particular person? And how does sense aid in obtaining what is not sensible?"

We say: Sense delivers to the imaginative power the likenesses of the sensible things and their forms — so that a man sees a thing, then closes his eyes and finds the form of the thing present with him matching what was observed, as though he were looking at it with the imaginative power, not the power of sense. This power is not for all animals; rather, among animals, some have the form of the sensed object vanish with the object's absence. The persistence of these forms belongs to the preserving power (al-quwwah al-ḥāfiẓah) for what is imprinted in the imagination. For a thing does not preserve what it receives by the very power by which it receives it — water receives an impression but does not preserve it, while wax receives and preserves. Reception is by moisture, preservation by dryness. Then when these images and forms are obtained in the imaginative power, the imaginative power studies them and does not study the external sensed objects. When it studies them, it finds with itself, for example, the form of a tree, an animal, and a stone, and finds them agreeing in corporeality and differing in animality. So it distinguishes what is common — namely corporeality — and makes it one universal, thus conceiving absolute body; and it takes what is different — namely animality — and makes it other universals stripped of their other concomitants. Then it knows what is essential and what is foreign, and knows that corporeality is essential to animality — for were it annihilated, its essence would be annihilated — and that whiteness is not so for animality. Thus the essential is distinguished from the non-essential, and the more general from the more specific, and these become the principles of specific conceptions.

So these universal simples are obtained by means of sensation, yet they are not sensible. Nor should one marvel that what is not sensible arises with sensation — for this exists in beasts. The mouse distinguishes the cat and apprehends it by sense and knows its enmity toward it; and the lamb apprehends the harmony of its mother with it and follows her. Enmity and harmony are not sensible; rather, they are apprehended by a power in the animal called the wahm (estimative faculty) or the discernment (mumayyiz). It is for the animal like the intellect — from particular imaginings it derives universal simples that correspond to the imagination in one respect and differ from it in another. We shall explain the respect of its correspondence and difference in the Book on the Judgments of Existence and Its Divisions.

The upshot of the discourse is that the primary sciences — in the simples by conception and in their relations by assent — arise in the soul from God, may He be exalted, or from one of His angels, upon the soul's attainment of the power of intellect, and upon the attainment of the likenesses of the sensible things in the imagination and its study of them. The rational power is like the seeing power in the eye, and the vision of the particular imaginings is like the focusing of the eye's gaze upon colored bodies. The shining of the light of the angel upon human souls resembles the shining of the light of a lamp upon colored bodies, or the shining of the sun's light upon them. And the attainment of knowledge of the relation of those simples resembles the attainment of sight through the composition of the colors of bodies. For this reason God, may He be exalted, likened this light by way of a sensible parable to a niche in which is a lamp. And if it has become clear to you that the soul is a self-subsistent substance, not a body nor imprinted in a body, then His saying, may He be exalted: {«زَيْتُونَةٍ لَا شَرْقِيَّةٍ وَلَا غَرْبِيَّةٍ»} ("an olive tree neither eastern nor western") corresponds to its reality in its being free from all directions. And if that has not been shown to you by way of inquiry, then the interpretation (ta'wīl) of this is carried out in another manner. The purpose of all this is that the manner of the attainment of the primary sciences — by conception and by assent — becomes clear to you. For the knowledge of that is among the most important of matters, and it is what we intended. Even though we have brought it in the context of refuting sophistry, this is one entry among the entries of the skeptics and the people of bewilderment, and we have uncovered it.

Among these is their saying: "The path you have mentioned for production (intāj) is of no benefit, for whoever knows the premises under your condition has already known the conclusion along with those premises — indeed, in the premises is the very conclusion. For whoever knows that the human is an animal and that the animal is a body has thereby known, in the totality of that, that the human is a body. So the knowledge that he is a body is not an additional knowledge acquired from these premises."

We say: The knowledge of the conclusion is an established knowledge additional to the knowledge of the two premises. As for the example of the human and the animal, we do not cite it except as a pure example. Benefit is derived from it only in what can be a sought and problematic matter — and this is not of that kind. Rather, it is possible that the conclusion not become evident to a man even though each of the two premises is evident to him. A man may know that every body is composite, and that every composite is originated, yet be heedless of the relation of origination to the body — namely, that the body is originated. For the relation of origination to the body is other than the relation of origination to the composite, and other than the relation of the composite to the body. Rather, it is a new knowledge that arises upon the attainment of the two premises and their joint presence in the mind, with the soul's attention directed toward seeking the conclusion.

If a questioner says: "If you know that every two is even, then is this thing in my hand even or not? If you say 'I do not know,' then your claim that every two is even is refuted — for it is two, and you did not know it is even. And if you say 'I know it,' then what is it?"

We say: One may answer this by saying that one who says "Every two is even" means "Every two that we know to be two is even" — and what is in your hand we have not known to be two. But this answer is corrupt. Rather, every two is in itself even, whether we know it or not. The correct answer is to say: If what is in your hand is two, then it is even. If you ask: "Is it two?" I say: "I do not know." This ignorance does not contradict my statement that every two is even. Rather, its contradictory is my saying "Every two is not even" or "Some two is not even." So one must ascertain whether it is two; if we know it is two, we know it is even — and we bring that to mind. And it is conceivable that one be heedless of the conclusion while the two premises are present. How many a person looks at a mule with a swollen belly and supposes it is pregnant! If one said to him: "Do you not know that this is a mule?" he would say: "Yes." And if one said: "Do you not know that the mule does not carry?" he would say: "Yes." Then if one said: "Why then were you heedless of the conclusion and supposed its opposite?" he would say: "Because I was heedless of composing the two premises and bringing them both together in the mind, directed toward seeking the conclusion." So it is disclosed by this that the conclusion, even though it is contained under the premises potentially — as the particulars are contained under the universals — is nevertheless an actual knowledge additional to them.

Among these is the saying of some skeptics: "If you seek by reflection a knowledge, then do you know that knowledge or not? If you know it, you did not seek it; and if you do not know it, then when you obtain it, how do you know it is what you sought? Are you not like one who seeks an escaped slave he does not know — if he finds him, he does not know whether he is the one or not?"

We say: The knowledge we seek we know in one respect and are ignorant of in another. We know it by conception actually, and we know it by assent potentially, and we wish to know it by assent actually. For when we seek the knowledge that the world is originated, we know "origination" and "world" by conception, and we are able to assent to it if a middle term appears between the world and origination — such as its accompaniment of originated things or other than that. For we know that what accompanies originated things is originated. If we know that the world accompanies originated things, we know actually that it is originated. And when we know it, we know it is what we sought — for had we not known it by conception before, we would not have known it was the sought object. And had we assented to it actually, we would not have sought it. This is like the escaped slave: we know him by conception and imagination in one respect and are ignorant of his location. When sense apprehends him in his location at once, we know he is the sought one. Had we not known him, we would not have recognized him upon finding him; and had we known him in every respect — that is, known his location — we would not have sought him.

This is what we wished to present of the perplexing, bewildering doubts of the Sophists. The purpose in presenting them was not to debate them, but to uncover these subtleties. For the seeker of certainty through the paths of demonstrations benefits immensely from knowing them. Otherwise, how is the Sophist to be debated? His very debate is an acknowledgment of the path of inquiry. Nor should one marvel at the belief in sophistry and bewilderment despite the clarity of the intelligibles — for that occurs only rarely, due to an affliction striking one's

chapters.arabic_text:
### | النظر الرابع في لواحق القياس

### | وهي فصول متفرقة بمعرفتها تتم معرفة البراهين

### | فصل في الفرق بين قياس العلة وقياس الدلالة

إعلم أن الحد الأوسط إن كان علة للحد الأكبر سماه الفقهاء قياس العلة،
وسماه المنطقيون برهان اللم أي ذكر ما يجاب به عن لم، وإن لم يكن علة سماه
الفقهاء قياس الدلالة. والمنطقيون سموه برهان اأن أي هو دليل على أن الحد
الأكبر موجود للأصغر من غير بيان علته. ومثال قياس العلة من المحسوسات
قولك: هذه الخشبة محترقة لأنها أصابتها النار، وهذا الإنسان شبعان لأنه أكل
الآن. وقياس الدلالة عكسه وهو أن يستدل بالنتيجة على المنتج فنقول: هذا
شبعان فإذا هو قريب العهد بالأكل، وهذه المرأة ذات لبن فهي قريبة العهد
بالولادة.
ومثاله من الفقه قولك: هذه عين نجسة فإذن لا تصح الصلاة معها، وقياس
الدلالة عكسه وهو أن نقول هذه عين لا تصح الصلاة معها فإذن هي نجسة.
وبالجملة الإستدلال بالنتيجة على المنتج يدل على وجوده فقط لا على علته،
فإنا نستدل بحدوث العالم على وجود المحدث، وبوجود الكتابة المنظومة على علم
الكاتب، ونجعل الكتابة حدا أوسط والعلم حدا أكبر، ونقول كل من كتب منظوما
فهو عالم بالكتابة، والكتابة ليست علة للعلم بل العلم أولى بأن نقدر عليته.
وكذلك إذا تلازمت نتيجتان بعلة واحدة جاز أن يستدل بإحدى النتيجتين على
الأخرى فيكون قياس دلالة. ومثاله من الفقه قولنا: إن الزنا لا يوجب
المحرمية فلا يوجب حرمة النكاح، فإن تحريم النكاح وحل النظر متلازمان، وهما
نتيجتان للوطء المقتضي لحرمة المصاهرة، فإذا ثبت تلازمهما لعلة واحدة دل
وجود إحداهما على وجود الأخرى، فإن اختلف شرطهما لم يمكن الإستدلال لإحتمال
افتراقهما في الشرط، وكما انقسم قياس الدلالة إلى نوعين فقياس العلة أيضا
ينقسم إلى قسمين: الأول: ما يكون الأوسط فيه علة للنتيجة ولا يكون علة
لوجود الأكبر في نفسه، كقولنا:
كل إنسان حيوان وكل حيوان جسم، فكل إنسان جسم.  فالإنسان إنما كان جسما من
قبل أنه حيوان والجسمية أولا للحيوان، ثم بسببه للإنسان، فإذا الحيوان علة
لحمل الجسم على الإنسان لا لوجود الجسمية، فإن الجسمية تتقدم بالذات في
ترتيب الأنواع والأجناس على الحيوان.
واعلم أن ما ثبت للنوع من حمل الجنس عليه، وكذا جنس الجنس، وكذا الفصول
والحود واللوازم إنما تكون من جهة الجنس، ويكون الجنس علة في حمله على
النوع لا في وجود ذات المحمول أعني محمول النتيجة.
والقسم الثاني: ما يكون علة لوجود الحد الأكبر على الإطلاق لا كهذا
المثال، وقد لا يكون على الإطلاق كالشيء الذي له علل متعددة، فإن آحاد
العلل لا يمكن أن تجعل علة للحد الأكبر مطلقا، بل هي علة في وقت مخصوص ومحل
مخصوص، ومثاله في الفقه؛ إن العدوان علة للتأثيم على الإطلاق، والزنا علة
للرجم على الإطلاق، والردة ليست علة للقتل على الإطلاق، فإن القتل يجب على
سبيل القصاص وغيره، ولكن تكون علة للقتل في حق شخص مخصوص، وذلك لا يخرجه عن
كونه قياس العلة.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Repetition and succession; a secondary occurrence following a primary one; hence 'cause' (ʿillah) as that which necessitates its effect in ordered sequence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The efficient cause in demonstrative reasoning — that which, when known, yields knowledge of the effect (ʿilm bi-al-ʿillah), distinct from mere concomitant indication.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) when the middle term truly produces the predicate; metaphorical (majāz) when it merely signals coexistence without causal efficacy.
- Root: د-ل-ل (d-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Guidance and direction; a marker (dalīl) that points beyond itself to something else.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): An epistemic sign establishing existence (thubūt) without penetrating to the ontological ground (ʿillah) of the thing signified.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The indicative sign functions as a trace (athar) of the cause, not the cause itself — a distinction pivotal to the present chapter.
- Root: ل-م-م (l-m-m) and أ-ن-ن (ʾ-n-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: 'Lim' answers 'why' (li-mā) — the reason; 'inn' answers 'that' (anna) — the fact.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Burhān al-limī establishes the reasoned fact (propter quid); burhān al-innī establishes the fact (quia) — the two demonstrative modes inherited from Aristotelian analytics.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The former ascends from cause to effect; the latter descends from effect to cause — a rhetorical inversion of epistemic priority.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq and Taʿlīl (Suspension and Causal Attribution) — When the particle 'li-anna' introduces a causal clause, it governs a nominal sentence in the accusative, binding the predicate to the subject through an explicit causal nexus; conversely, 'fa-idhan' marks an inferential apodosis, where the consequent is drawn from the antecedent by way of indication, not causation.
chapters.translation:
Know that if the middle term is a cause of the major term, the jurists (fuqahāʾ) call it the syllogism of cause (qiyās al-ʿillah), and the logicians call it the demonstrative proof of the 'why' (burhān al-limī) — that is, the mention of that by which one answers the question 'why'. If it is not a cause, the jurists call it the syllogism of indication (qiyās al-dalālah), and the logicians call it the demonstrative proof of the 'that' (burhān al-innī) — namely, it is an indication that the major term inheres in the minor term without any exposition of its cause.

An example of the syllogism of cause from the domain of sense-perception is your statement: 'This piece of wood is burnt because fire touched it,' and 'This man is satiated because he has just eaten.' The syllogism of indication is its inverse — namely, that one infers from the conclusion to that which produced it. Thus we say: 'This man is satiated; therefore he is recently acquainted with eating,' and 'This woman has milk; therefore she is recently acquainted with childbirth.'

Its example from jurisprudence is your statement: 'This is an impure substance (ʿayn najisah); therefore prayer is not valid with it.' The syllogism of indication is its inverse — namely, that we say: 'This is a substance with which prayer is not valid; therefore it is impure.'

In sum, inferring from the conclusion to that which produced it indicates only its existence, not its cause. For we infer from the origination (ḥudūth) of the world to the existence of the Originator (al-muḥdith), and from the existence of well-ordered writing to the knowledge of the writer. We make writing the middle term and knowledge the major term, and we say: 'Everyone who writes in an ordered manner is knowledgeable in writing.' Yet writing is not a cause of knowledge; rather, knowledge is more deserving of being posited as the cause.

Likewise, if two conclusions are necessarily concomitant (mutalāzimān) through a single cause, it is permissible to infer from one of the two conclusions to the other, and this would be a syllogism of indication. Its example from jurisprudence is our statement: 'Fornication (zinā) does not necessitate the prohibition of marriage (ḥurmat al-nikāḥ),' for the prohibition of marriage and the permissibility of gazing (ḥill al-naẓar) are necessarily concomitant, and both are two conclusions of the act of intercourse (waṭʾ) which entails the prohibition of affinity (ḥurmat al-muṣāharah). So when their concomitance through a single cause is established, the existence of one of them indicates the existence of the other. But if their conditions differ, inference becomes impossible, due to the possibility of their divergence in condition.

Just as the syllogism of indication divides into two types, so too the syllogism of cause divides into two divisions. The first: that in which the middle term is a cause of the conclusion but is not a cause of the existence of the major term in itself — as in our statement: 'Every human is an animal, and every animal is a body; therefore every human is a body.' For the human is a body only by virtue of being an animal, and corporeality (al-jismiyyah) belongs first to the animal, then through it to the human. Thus the animal is a cause of the predication of 'body' upon the human, not of the existence of corporeality — for corporeality is prior in essence (bi-al-dhāt) in the ordering of species and genera to the animal.

Know that whatever is established for a species regarding the predication of its genus upon it — and likewise the genus of the genus, and likewise the differentiae (fuṣūl), accidents (khawāṣṣ), and necessary concomitants (lawāzim) — is only by way of the genus. The genus is a cause in its predication upon the species, not in the existence of the essence of the predicate — I mean, the predicate of the conclusion.

The second division: that which is a cause of the existence of the major term absolutely (ʿalā al-iṭlāq), not like this example. And it may not be absolute — such as a thing that has multiple causes, for no single one of the causes can be made a cause of the major term absolutely; rather, it is a cause in a specific time and a specific locus. Its example in jurisprudence: transgression (ʿudwān) is a cause of sinfulness (taʾthīm) absolutely; fornication is a cause of stoning (rajm) absolutely; but apostasy (riddah) is not a cause of killing absolutely — for killing is obligatory by way of retribution (qiṣāṣ) and otherwise — rather, it is a cause of killing with respect to a specific person. And this does not remove it from being a syllogism of cause.

chapters.title_en: Section 42 — On the Elucidation of Certainty (Bayān al-Yaqīn)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فصل في بيان اليقين

البرهان الحقيقي ما يفيد شيئا لا يتصور تغيره، ويكون ذلك بحسب مقدمات
البرهان فإنها تكون يقينية أبدية، لا تستحيل ولا تتغير أبدا، وأعني بذلك أن
الشيء لا يتغير
وأن غفل إنسان عنه كقولنا: الكل أعظم من الجزء والأشياء المساوية لشيء
واحد متساوية وأمثالها، فالنتيجة الحاصلة منها أيضا تكون يقينية، والعلم
اليقيني هو أن تعرف أن الشيء بصفة كذا مقترنا بالتصديق بأنه لا يمكن ان لا
يكون كذا، فإنك لو أخطرت ببالك إمكان الخطأ فيه والذهول عنه لم ينقدح ذلك
في نفسك أصلا، فإن إقترن به تجوز الخطأ وإمكانه فليس بيقيني؛ فهكذا ينبغي
أن تعرف نتائج البرهان، فإن عرفته معرفة على حد قولنا فقيل لك خلافه حكاية
عن أعظم خلق الله مرتبة وأجلهم في النظر والعقليات درجة، وأورث ذلك عندك
احتمالا، فليس اليقين تاما، بل لو نقل عن نبي صادق نقيضه فينبغي أن يقطع
بكذب الناقل أو بتأويل اللفظ المسموع عنه، ولا يخطر  ببالك إمكان الصدق، فإن
لم يقبل التأويل فشك في نبوة من حكى عنه بخلاف ماعقلت إن كان ما عقلته
يقينا فإن شككت في صدقه لم يكن يقينك تاما.
فإن قلت: ربما ظهر لي برهان صدقة ثم سمعت منه ما يناقض برهانا قامعندي.
فأقول: وجود هذا يستحيل كقول القائل لو تناقضت الأخبار المتواترة فما
السبيل فيها كما لو تواتر وجود مكة وعدمها؟ فهذا محال، فالتناقض في
البراهين الجامعة للشروط التي ذكرناها محال، فإن رأيتها متناقضة فاعلم أن
أحدهما أو كلاهما لم يتحقق فيه الشروط المذكورة فتفقد مظان الغلط والمثارات
السبع التي فصلناها، وأكثر الغلط يكون في المبادرة إلى تسليم مقدمات
البرهان على أنها أولية ولا تكون أولية، بل ربما تكون محمودة مشهورة أو
وهمية،
ولا ينبغي أن تسلم المقدمات ما لم يكن اليقين فيها على الحد الذي وصفناه.
وكما يظن فيما ليست أولية أنها أولية فقد يظن بالأوليات أنها ليست أولية
فيشكك فيها، ولا يتشكك في الأوليات إلا بزوال الذهن عن الفطرة السليمة،
لمخالطة بعض المتكلمين المتعصبين للمذاهب الفاسدة بمجاحدة الجليات حتى تأنس
النفس بسماعها فيشك في اليقيني، كما أنه قد يتكرر على سمعه ما ليس يقينا من
المحمودات فتذعن للتصديق به وتظن أنه يقيني بكثرة سماعه، وهذا أعظم مثارات
الغلط ويعز في العقلاء من يحسن الإحتراز من الإغترار به.
فإن قلت فمثل هذا اليقين عزيز يقل وجوده فتقل به المقدمات.
قلنا: ما يتساعد فيه الوهم والعقل من الحسابيات والهندسيات والحسيات
كثير، فيكثر فيها مثل هذه اليقينيات، وكذا المعقولات التي لا تحاذيها
الوهميات فأما العقليات الصرفة المتعلقة بالنظر في الإلهيات ففيها بعض مثل
هذه اليقينيات، ولا يبلغ اليقين فيها إلى الحد الذي ذكرناه إلا بطول ممارسة
العقليات، وفطام العقل عن الوهميات والحسيات وإيناسها بالعقليات المحضة،
وكلما كان النظر فيها أكثر والجد في طلبها أتم كانت المعارف فيها إلى حد
اليقين التام أقرب، ثم من طالت ممارسته وحصلت له ملكة بتلك المعارف لا يقدر
على إفحام الخصم فيه ولا يقدر على تنزيل  المسترشد منزلة نفسه، بمجرد ذكر ما
عنده إلا بأن يرشده إلى أن يسلك مسلكه في ممارسة العلوم وطول التأمل حتى
يصل إلى ما وصل إليه إن كان صحيح الحدس ثاقب العقل صافي الذكاء، وإن فارقه
في الذكاء أو في الحدس أو تولي الإعتبار الذي تولاه لم يصل إلى ما وصل
إليه، وعند ذلك يقابل ما يحكيه عن نفسه بالإنكار ويشتغل بالتهجين
والإستبعاد، وسبيل العارف البصير أن يعرض عنه صفحا بل لا يبث إليه أسرار ما
عنده، فإن ذلك أسلم لجانبه وأقطع لشغب الجهال، فما كل ما يرى يقال بل صدور
الأحرار قبور الأسرار.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ي-ق-ن (ya-qāf-nūn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firmness, stability, and the absence of doubt; certainty as a settled conviction that admits no wavering.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Certainty (yaqīn) is the cognition (maʿrifah) of a thing as it truly is, conjoined with the affirmation (taṣdīq) that its contrary is impossible—distinct from mere opinion (ẓann) or conjecture.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes unshakeable conviction; metaphorical (majāz) usage applies to strong belief that still tolerates theoretical error.
- Root: ب-ر-ه-ن (bā-rā-hā-nūn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A clear proof or demonstration; that which renders a matter evident and manifest.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Burhān is a syllogism (qiyās) composed of certain premises (muqaddimāt yaqīniyyah) yielding a necessary conclusion—the highest form of demonstration in the theoretical sciences.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: an evidentiary argument; metaphorical: any sign or indication that leads to knowledge.
- Root: ص-د-ق (ṣād-dāl-qāf)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Truthfulness and veracity; the correspondence of speech with reality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taṣdīq is the assent of the heart affirming a proposition as true—the cognitive act that constitutes belief or conviction.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: affirming truth; metaphorical: the heart's submission to a report.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (law, fa-in, fa-idhā) and exceptive phrases (illā bi-, mā lam) to delineate the precise conditions under which certainty obtains or fails, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the logical force of the argument.
chapters.translation:
I say: The true demonstration (al-burhān al-ḥaqīqī) is that which yields something whose change is inconceivable; and this is in accordance with the premises of the demonstration, for they are certain (yaqīniyyah) and eternal (abadiyyah)—they neither undergo alteration nor change ever. By this I mean that the thing does not change, even if a person is heedless of it—such as our saying: "The whole is greater than the part," and "Things equal to one and the same thing are equal to each other," and the like. Thus, the conclusion (al-natījah) produced from them is also certain. And certain knowledge (al-ʿilm al-yaqīnī) is that you know that a thing possesses such-and-such an attribute, conjoined with the affirmation (taṣdīq) that it is impossible for it not to be so. For if you entertain in your mind the possibility of error concerning it or heedlessness of it, that [possibility] would not flash upon your soul at all. But if the possibility and likelihood of error is conjoined with it, then it is not certain. In this manner you ought to know the conclusions of demonstration. For if you know it in the manner we have stated, and then someone tells you the contrary of it, narrating it from the greatest of Allah's creation in rank and the most eminent of them in theoretical and rational matters, and this engenders in you a possibility [of its truth], then the certainty is not complete. Rather, even if the contrary of it were transmitted from a truthful prophet (nabī ṣādiq), you ought to decisively affirm the falsehood of the transmitter or the allegorical interpretation (taʾwīl) of the heard utterance—and the possibility of its truth should not cross your mind. For if it does not admit of interpretation, then you should doubt the prophethood of the one from whom it is narrated, contrary to what you have rationally grasped—if what you grasped was certain. For if you doubt his truthfulness, your certainty is not complete.

If you say: "Perhaps a demonstration of his truthfulness has appeared to me, then I heard from him something that contradicts a demonstration established in my mind." I say: The existence of this is impossible—like one who says: "If the mutawātir reports (al-akhbār al-mutawātirah) contradicted one another, what would be the way [to resolve them]?"—as if the existence of Mecca and its non-existence were both transmitted by tawātur. This is impossible. Thus, contradiction among demonstrations that fulfill the conditions we have mentioned is impossible. If you see them as contradictory, then know that one of them—or both—has not actually fulfilled the mentioned conditions. So examine the loci of error (maẓān al-ghalaṭ) and the seven sources (al-mathārāt al-sabʿ) which we have detailed. Most error occurs in hastening to accept the premises of a demonstration as primary (awwaliyyah) when they are not primary; rather, they may be commendable (maḥmūdah), well-known (mashhūrah), or imaginary (wahmiyyah). And you ought not to accept premises unless certainty in them is at the limit we have described.

And just as one may suppose that what is not primary is primary, so too one may suppose that primary [truths] are not primary, and thus cast doubt upon them. But one does not doubt primary truths except by the mind's departure from sound natural disposition (al-fiṭrah al-salīmah)—due to mixing with certain theologians (mutakallimīn) who are fanatical for corrupt doctrines, by denying self-evident truths (mujāḥadah al-jaliyyāt), until the soul becomes accustomed to hearing [such denials] and thus doubts the certain. Likewise, what is not certain—from among the commendable [opinions]—may be repeated upon one's hearing, and the soul yields to affirming it and supposes it certain due to the frequency of hearing it. This is the greatest of the sources of error; and rare among the intelligent is one who excels in guarding against being deceived by it.

If you say: "Such certainty is rare; its existence is scarce, and thus the premises [available] become scarce." We say: That in which imagination (wahm) and intellect (ʿaql) concur—from among the arithmetical, geometrical, and sensory [truths]—is abundant, so such certainties abound therein. Likewise, the intelligibles (maʿqūlāt) that are not paralleled by imaginary [constructs]. As for the pure rational matters (al-ʿaqliyyāt al-ṣirfah) pertaining to inquiry into the divine things (al-ilāhiyyāt), there is in them some measure of such certainties, but certainty therein does not reach the limit we have mentioned except through prolonged practice of the rational sciences, weaning the intellect from imaginary and sensory [attachments], and accustoming it to pure rational matters. And the more the inquiry therein is abundant, and the more earnest the striving in seeking it, the closer the cognitions therein draw to the limit of complete certainty. Then, whoever has prolonged his practice and acquired a faculty (malakah) through those cognitions—he is not able to silence the opponent (ifḥām al-khaṣm) concerning it, nor is he able to bring the seeker of guidance (al-mustarshid) down to his own station, merely by mentioning what he possesses—except by guiding him to traverse his own path in practicing the sciences and prolonging reflection, until he reaches what he has reached—if he has sound intuition (ḥads), penetrating intellect, and pure acumen. But if he differs from him in acumen or in intuition, or neglects the reflection (al-iʿtibār) that he undertook, he will not reach what he has reached. At that point, he confronts what he narrates of himself with denial, and occupies himself with disparagement and deeming it remote. The way of the knowing seer (al-ʿārif al-baṣīr) is to turn away from him entirely—nay, he should not divulge to him the secrets of what he possesses. For that is safer for his standing and more decisive against the clamor of the ignorant. For not everything that is seen is spoken; rather, the breasts of the free are the graves of secrets.

chapters.title_en: On the Principal Categories of Inquiry and the Meaning of Essential (Dhātī) and Primary (Awwalī)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فصل في أمهات المطالب

إعلم أن المطلوبات من العلوم بالسؤال عنها أربعة أقسام بسبب إنتساب كل
واحد إلى الصيغة التي بها يسأل عنه: الأول: مطلب " هل " وهذا السؤال أعني
صيغة هل، يتوجه نحو طلب وجود الشيء في نفسه كقولنا: الله موجود وهل الخلاء
موجود؟ أو نحو وجود صفة أو حال لشيء كقولنا: هل الله مريد وهل العالم حادث؟
فيسمى الأول مطلب هل مطلقا والثاني مطلب هل مقيدا.
والثاني: مطلب " ما " ويعرف به التصور دون التصديق، وذلك إما بحسب الإسم
كقولك: ما الخلاء وما عنقاء مغرب؟ أي ما الذي تريد باسمه؟ وهذا يتقدم كل
مطلب فإن من لم يفهم معنى العالم والحدوث لا يمكن أن يسأل: هل العالم
موجود؟ ومن لم يتصور معنى الدال لا يمكنه أن يسأله عن وجود. وإما أن يكون
الطلب بحسب حقيقة الذات كقولك: ما الإنسان وما العقار؟
وأنت تطلب به حده إذا عرفت أن المراد باسم العقار هو الخمر، وهذا يتأخر
عن مطلب " هل " فإن من لا يعتقد للخمر وجودا لا يسأل عن حده.
والثالث: مطلب " لم " وهو طلب العلة لجواب هل كقولك: لم كان العالم
حادثا؟ وهو إما طلب علة التصديق كقولك: لم قلت أن الله موجود؟ فإنه لا يطلب
العلة في وجوده بل العلة في وقوع التصديق بوجوده، وهو برهان الآن بلغة
المنطقيين، وقياس الدلالة بلغة المتكلمين، وإما طلب علة الوجود  كقولك لم
حدث العالم؟ فنقول: لإرادة محدثة.
والرابع مطلب: " أي " وهو الذي يطلب به تميز الشيء عما عداه، فهذه أمهات
المطالب والأسئلة. فأما مطلب " أين ومتى وكيف " فليست من الأمهات فإنها
داخلة بالقوة تحت مطلب " هل " المقيد إن وقع التفطن له بالسؤال بصيغة هل،
وإن لم يقع كانت مطالب خارجة عما عددناها.

### | فصل في بيان معنى الذاتي والأولي

أما الذاتي فيطلق على وجهين: أحدهما أن يكون المحمول مأخوذا في حد
الموضوع مقوما له داخلا في حقيقة كقولنا: الإنسان حيوان، فيقالك الحيوان
ذاتي للإنسان أي هو مقوم له كما سبق بيانه.
وإما أن يكون الموضوع مأخوذا في حد المحمول كقولنا: بعض الحيوان إنسانن
فإن المحمول هو الإنسان ههنا لا الحيوان، والإنسان لا يؤخذ في حد الحيوان
بل الحيوان يؤخذ في حد الإنسان، فكل شيئين لا يؤخذ أحدهما في حد الآخر فليس
أحدهما ذاتيا للآخر. وقد يمثل بالفطوسة في الأنف فإنه ذاتي للأنف بالمعنى
الأخير، إذ لا يمكن تحديد الفطوسة إلا بذكر الأنف في حده.
وأما الأولى فإنه يقال أيضا على وجهين: أحدهما ما هو أولي في العقل أي لا
يحتاج في معرفته إلى وسط كقولنا: الإثنان أكثر من الواحد. والثاني أن يكون
بحيث لا يمكن إيجاب المحمول أو سلبه على معنى آخر أعم من الموضوع؟ فإذا
قلنا: الإنسان يمرض ويصح، لم يكن أوليا له بهذا المعنى إذ يقال على ما هو
أعم منه وهو الحيوان: نعم هو للحيوان أولى، لأنه لا يقال على ما هو أعم
منه، وهو الجسم؛ وكذلك قبول الإنتقال للحيوان ليس بأولى إذ يقال على ماهو
أعم منه وهو الجسم، فإنه لو إرتفع الحيوان بقي قبول الإنتقال، ولو ارتفع
الجسم لم يبق.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط ل ب (ṭ-l-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Seeking, demanding, or requesting something with intent; the act of pursuit toward an object of need.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, ṭalab denotes the intellectual quest for a proposition's truth or a thing's quiddity, distinguishing existential from conceptual seeking.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of an active pursuit; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the soul's inclination toward knowledge as if it were a physical chase.
- Root: ه ل (h-l) — interrogative particle
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A question marker for existence or occurrence; its core is the demand for affirmation or negation of a state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, "hal" probes wujūd (existence) either absolutely or conditionally, forming the basis of tasdīq (assent).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal as a grammatical tool for interrogation; metaphorical when extended to rhetorical questioning of essence.
- Root: م ا (m-a) — interrogative for quiddity
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: What? — seeking definition, name, or essence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "Mā" seeks taṣawwur (conception) without assent, distinguishing nominal from real definition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for asking about a thing's identity; metaphorical when used to elicit a boundary (ḥadd) of a known referent.
- Root: ل م (l-m) — interrogative for cause
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Why? — demanding a reason or cause.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "Lim" targets ʿillah (cause), either of assent (burhān al-ān) or of existence (ʿillat al-wujūd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for causal inquiry; metaphorical when applied to epistemic justification rather than ontological causation.
- Root: أ ي (a-y) — interrogative for distinction
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Which? — seeking differentiation among alternatives.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): "Ayy" isolates a thing's unique characteristic (tamyīz) against what is other than it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for selection; metaphorical for logical discrimination in definition.
- Root: ذ ا ت (dh-a-t) — essence
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Self, substance, or that which constitutes a thing's reality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Dhātī is that which enters the quiddity (māhiyyah) of a thing as a constituent (muqawwim), either as predicate in subject or subject in predicate.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for intrinsic constitution; metaphorical for accidental attribution.
- Root: أ و ل (a-w-l) — first, primary
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Beginning, foremost, or that which precedes others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Awwalī in logic means self-evident (badīhī) in the intellect, or universally applicable without a broader middle term.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for temporal or ontological priority; metaphorical for epistemic immediacy.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Jumlah (Ellipsis and Clause Reconstruction) — In complex interrogative structures like "هل الخلاء موجود؟", the predicate is governed by the implicit copula of existence, requiring the reader to reconstruct the full nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ-khabar) for accurate parsing.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the objects of inquiry among the sciences, when questioned about them, are four divisions, owing to the relation of each one to the formula by which it is asked. The first: the inquiry of "whether" (hal). This question — I mean the formula "hal" — is directed either toward seeking the existence of a thing in itself, as when we say: God is existent, and is the void existent? Or toward the existence of an attribute or state of a thing, as when we say: Is God willing, and is the world originated (ḥādith)? Thus the first is called the absolute inquiry of "whether" (hal muṭlaqan), and the second the restricted inquiry of "whether" (hal muqayyadan).

The second: the inquiry of "what" (mā). By it is known conception (taṣawwur) without assent (taṣdīq). This is either according to the name, as when you say: What is the void, and what is the Anqā of the West? — i.e., what do you intend by its name? And this precedes every inquiry, for whoever does not understand the meaning of "world" and "origination" cannot ask: Is the world existent? And whoever does not conceive the meaning of "signifier" cannot ask about its existence. Or the inquiry is according to the reality of the essence, as when you say: What is man, and what is wine (al-ʿiqār)? You seek thereby its definition (ḥadd), when you know that the intended meaning of the name "al-ʿiqār" is wine. And this is posterior to the inquiry of "whether," for whoever does not affirm the existence of wine does not ask about its definition.

The third: the inquiry of "why" (lima). It is the seeking of the cause (ʿillah) for the answer to "whether," as when you say: Why was the world originated? It is either a seeking of the cause of assent, as when you say: Why did you say that God is existent? For it does not seek the cause in His existence, but rather the cause of the occurrence of assent to His existence — and this is the "proof of the now" (burhān al-ān) in the language of the logicians, and the "argument of indication" (qiyās al-dalālah) in the language of the theologians. Or it is a seeking of the cause of existence, as when you say: Why did the world originate? We say: Due to an originated will (irādah muḥdathah).

The fourth: the inquiry of "which" (ayy). It is that by which is sought the distinction of a thing from what is other than it. These, then, are the principal categories of inquiries and questions. As for the inquiry of "where," "when," and "how," they are not among the principal categories, for they fall potentially under the restricted inquiry of "whether," if one becomes attentive to them by questioning with the formula "hal." And if not, they are inquiries external to what we have enumerated.

As for the essential (dhātī), it is said in two respects: One of them is that the predicate is taken into the definition (ḥadd) of the subject, constituting it (muqawwim), entering into its reality — as when we say: Man is animal. Thus it is said that animal is essential to man, i.e., it constitutes him, as has been previously explained. Or the subject is taken into the definition of the predicate, as when we say: Some animal is man. For the predicate here is man, not animal; and man is not taken into the definition of animal, but rather animal is taken into the definition of man. So any two things of which one is not taken into the definition of the other — neither of them is essential to the other. And it may be exemplified by snubness (al-fatūsah) in the nose, for it is essential to the nose in the latter sense, since snubness cannot be defined except by mentioning the nose in its definition.

As for the primary (awwalī), it is also said in two respects: One of them is what is primary in the intellect, i.e., it does not need a middle term (wasaṭ) for its cognition — as when we say: Two is more than one. The second is that it be such that the predicate cannot be affirmed or negated of a meaning more general than the subject. So when we say: Man becomes ill and recovers, this is not primary to him in this sense, for it is said of what is more general than him, namely animal. Yes, it is primary to animal, because it is not said of what is more general than it, namely body. Likewise, the receptivity of locomotion for animal is not primary, for it is said of what is more general than it, namely body — for if animal were removed, the receptivity of locomotion would remain, but if body were removed, it would not remain.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فصل فيما يلتئم به أمر البراهين

وهي ثلاثة: مبادي وموضوعات ومسائل. فالموضوعات نعني بها ما يبرهن فيها،
والمسائل ما يبرهن عليها، والمبادي ما يبرهن بها. والمراد بالمبادي
المقدمات، وقد ذكرناها.
وأما الموضوعات فهي الأمور التي توضع في العلوم وتطلب أعراضها الذاتية،
أعني الذاتية بالمعنى الثاني من  المعنيين المذكورين، ولكل علم موضوع:
فموضوع الهندسة المقدار، وموضوع الحساب العدد، وموضوع لنحو لغة العرب منجهة
ما يختلف إعرابها، وموضوع الفقه أفعال المكلفين من جهة ما ينهى عنها أو
يؤمر بها أو يباح أو يندب أو يكره، وموضوع أصول الفقه أحكام الشرع، أعني
الوجوب والحظر والإباحة من جهة ما تدرك به من أدلتها، وموضوع المنطق تمييز
المعقولات وتلخيص المعاني.
وأما المسائل فهي القضايا الخاصة بكل علم، التي يطلب المعرفة في العلوم
بأحد طرفيها: إما النفي وإما الإثبات كقولنا في الحساب: هذا العدد إمازوج
او فرد، وفي الهندسة: هذا المقدار مساو أو مباين، وفي الفقه: هذا الفعل
حلال أوحرام أو واجب،
وفي العلم الإلهي: هذا الموجود قديم أو حادث وهذا الموجود له سبب أو ليس
له سبب.
والمقصود أن محمول المسائل إن كان مطلوبا بالنظر فلا يجوز أن يكون ذاتيا
للموضوع بالمعنى الأول، لأنه إذا كان كذلك كان معلوما قبل العلم بالموضوع،
فإن الحيوان الذي هو ذاتي للإنسان بمعنى أنه وجد في حده لا يجوز أن يكون
مطلوبا فغن من عرف الإنسان فقد عرف كونه حيوانا قبله لا محالة، فإن أجزاء
الحد يتقدم العلم بها على العلم بالمحدود، ولكن الذاتي بالمعنى الثاني وهو
المطلوب، وأما كل محمول ليس المعنى الثاني ولا بالمعنى الأول فإنه يسمى
غريبا كقولنا في الهندسة عند النظر في الخطوط: هذا الخط حسن أو قبيح، لأن
الحسن والقبح لا يؤخذ في حد الخط ولا الخط في حده، بل الذاتي لذاته مستقيم
أو منحني وأمثاله. وكذا قولنا في الطب: هذا الجرح مستدير أو مربع، فإنه
محمول غريب للجرح إذ لا يؤخذ واحد منهما في حد الآخر، وإنما هو ذاتي
للأشكال.
وقد يكون المحمول ذاتيا للموضوع بالمعنى الثاني، ولكن يكون غريبا
بالإضافة إلى العلم الذي يستعمل فيه كقولنا في الفقه: هذه الحركة سريعة أو
بطيئة، فإن السرعة والبطء ذاتي للحركة، ولكن إنما يطلب في العلم الطبيعي،
والمطلوب في الفقه ذاتي آخر وهو كونه واجبا أو محظورا أو مباحا.
وإذا قلنا  في العلم الطبيعي: هذا الفعل حلال أو حرام
كان غريبا من العلم. فإن قيل: فهل يجوز أن يكون المحمول في المقدمتين
ذاتيا بالمعنى الأول؟ قلنا: لا، لأنه إن كان كذلك تكون النتيجة معلومة،
فإذا قلنا: الإنسان حيوان والحيوان جسم فالإنسان جسم، كان العلم بالنتيجة
غير مطلوب فإن منعرف الإنسان فقد عرف جميع أجزاء حده وهو الجسم والحيوان.
نعم لا يبعد أن لا يكون كل واحد ذاتيا بالمعنى الثاني، بل إن كان أحدهما
ذاتيا بالمعنى الثاني كفى، سواء كان هي الصغرى أو الكبرى.
فإن قيل: فلم قلتم أن الذاتي بالمعنى الأول لا يكون مطلوبا، ونحن نطلب
العلم بأن النفس جوهر أم لا، والجوهرية للنفس ذاتية إذ منعرف النفس فيعرف
كونه جوهرا إن كان جوهرا؟ قلنا: من عرف النفس لم يتصور منه طلب كونه جوهرا،
إذ معرفة جوهريته سابقة على المعرفة به، لكنا إذا طلبنا أن النفس جوهر أم
لا لم يكن عرفنا من النفس إلا أمرا عارضا له وهو المحرك والمدرك، ويكون ذلك
مثل الأبيض للثلج، والمطلوب جنس المعروض له وهو غير مقوم لماهية العارض،
أعني الجوهرية ليس مقوما للمدرك والمحرك تقويم الذاتيات، وكذلك كلما حصل
عندنا خياله أو إسمه لا حقيقته، أمكن أن نطلب جنس ذلك حصل لنا إسمه أو
خياله، فأما على غير هذا الوجه فلا يمكن.

### | فصل في حل شبهة في القياس الدوري

فإن قال قائل: فلم قضيتم ببطلان البرهان الدوري؟ ومعلوم أنه إذا سأل
الإنسان عن الأسباب والمسببات على ما أجرى الله سنته بإرتباط البعض منها
بالبعض ففيها ما يرجع بالدور إلى الأول إذ يقال: لم كان السحاب؟ فيقال:
لأنه كان بخارا فكثف وانعقد. فقيل: لم كان البخار؟ فيقال: لأن الأرض كانت
ندية فأثر الحر فيها فتبخرت أجزاء الرطوبة وتصعدت. فقيل: ولم كانت الأرض
ندية؟ فقيل: لأنه كان مطر. فقيل: ولم كان المطر؟ فقيل: لأنه كان سحاب. فرجع
بالدور إلى السحاب فكأنه قيل: لم كان السحاب؟ فقلت: لأنه كان سحاب. والدوري
باطل سواء كان الحد المتكرر تخلله  واسطة أو وسائط، أو لم يتخلل فنقول: ليس
هذا هو الدوري الباطل، إنما الباطل أن يؤخذ الشيء في بيان نفسه بعينه بأن
يقال: لم كان هذا السحاب؛ فيعلل بما يرجع بالآخرة إلى التعليل بهذا السحاب
بعينه؛ فأما أن يرجع إلى التعليل بسحاب آخر فالعلة غير المعلول بالعدد، إلا
أنه مساو له في النوع، ولا يبعد أن يكون سحاب بعينه علة لسحاب آخر بواسطة
ترطيب الأرض، ثم تصعد البخار ثم انعقاده سحابا آخر.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ر-ه-ن (burhān)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Clear, decisive proof; that which renders a matter evident and incontrovertible.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Demonstration as apodictic proof yielding certain knowledge (yaqīn), distinct from dialectic (jadal) and rhetoric (khiṭābah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense — a proof that is self-evident in its force; metaphorical extension to any conclusive argument.
- Root: و-ض-ع (waḍʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To place, set down, establish as a foundation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The subject-matter (mawḍūʿ) of a science — that which is posited as the domain of inquiry, whose essential accidents (aʿrāḍ dhātiyyah) are sought.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical placement; metaphorical — the conceptual "placement" of a topic as the substrate of a discipline.
- Root: ذ-ا-ت (dhāt)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Self, essence, that which a thing is in itself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Two senses of "essential" (dhātī): (1) constitutive of the quiddity (e.g., animal for man, entering his definition); (2) a necessary attribute following from the essence but not entering the definition (e.g., capacity for laughter in man).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the self; metaphorical — that which pertains to a thing's nature as opposed to accidental (ʿaraḍī).
- Root: د-و-ر (dawr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Circularity, rotation, returning to the point of origin.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In logic — a vicious circle in proof where the conclusion presupposes the premise and vice versa.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — circular motion; metaphorical — circular reasoning.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition (al-Sharṭ) — The conditional structure "إذا كان كذا... فإنه كذا" governs the logical dependence of the apodosis on the protasis, mirroring the syllogistic relation of premises to conclusion.
chapters.translation:
I say: The matters by which the composition of demonstrations is perfected are three: principles (mabādiʾ), subjects (mawḍūʿāt), and problems (masāʾil). By "subjects" I mean that in which demonstration is made; by "problems" that about which demonstration is made; and by "principles" that by which demonstration is made. By "principles" is meant the premises, which we have already discussed.

As for the subjects, they are the things posited in the sciences whose essential accidents (aʿrāḍ dhātiyyah) are sought — I mean "essential" in the second of the two senses mentioned. Every science has a subject: the subject of geometry is magnitude (miqdār); the subject of arithmetic is number (ʿadad); the subject of grammar is the Arabic language insofar as its inflection (iʿrāb) varies; the subject of jurisprudence (fiqh) is the acts of the legally responsible person (mukallaf) insofar as they are prohibited, commanded, permitted, recommended, or discouraged; the subject of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) is the rulings of the Law (aḥkām al-sharʿ) — namely, obligation, prohibition, and permission — insofar as they are known through their evidences; and the subject of logic is the discernment of the intelligibles (tamyīz al-maʿqūlāt) and the distillation of meanings (talkhīṣ al-maʿānī).

As for the problems, they are the propositions specific to each science, whose knowledge is sought in the sciences with respect to one of their two sides: either negation or affirmation — as when we say in arithmetic: "This number is either even or odd"; in geometry: "This magnitude is either equal or unequal"; in jurisprudence: "This act is lawful, unlawful, or obligatory"; and in the divine science (al-ʿilm al-ilāhī): "This existent is eternal or originated (qadīm aw ḥādith)" and "This existent has a cause or has no cause."

The point is that if the predicate of a problem is sought by inquiry, it cannot be essential (dhātī) to the subject in the first sense — for if it were so, it would be known prior to the knowledge of the subject. For "animal," which is essential to "man" in the sense that it enters his definition, cannot be something sought; for whoever knows man has necessarily known that he is an animal beforehand, since the parts of the definition are known prior to the knowledge of the defined thing. Rather, what is sought is the essential in the second sense. As for any predicate that is neither essential in the second sense nor in the first, it is called "foreign" (gharīb) — as when we say in geometry, when examining lines: "This line is beautiful or ugly," for beauty and ugliness are not taken into the definition of the line, nor is the line taken into their definition. Rather, what is essential to the line in itself is being straight or curved and the like. Similarly, when we say in medicine: "This wound is round or square," this is a foreign predicate of the wound, since neither of these is taken into the definition of the other; rather, it is essential to shapes.

It may happen that a predicate is essential to the subject in the second sense, yet is foreign with respect to the science in which it is employed — as when we say in jurisprudence: "This movement is swift or slow," for swiftness and slowness are essential to movement, but they are sought only in natural science (al-ʿilm al-ṭabīʿī). What is sought in jurisprudence is another essential attribute, namely, its being obligatory, prohibited, or permissible. And if we say in natural science: "This act is lawful or unlawful," it would be foreign to that science.

If it is said: "Is it permissible for the predicate in the two premises to be essential in the first sense?" I say: No — for if it were so, the conclusion would already be known. Thus, when we say "Man is an animal" and "The animal is a body," so "Man is a body," the knowledge of the conclusion is not sought; for whoever knows man has already known all the parts of his definition, namely, body and animal. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that not every one of them be essential in the second sense; rather, if one of them is essential in the second sense, that suffices — whether it be the minor or the major premise.

If it is said: "Why do you hold that the essential in the first sense is not sought, when we seek to know whether the soul is a substance or not — and substantiality (jawhariyyah) is essential to the soul, since whoever knows the soul knows that it is a substance, if it is a substance?" I say: Whoever knows the soul cannot be conceived as seeking its being a substance, for the knowledge of its substantiality is prior to the knowledge of it. Rather, when we seek whether the soul is a substance or not, we have not known of the soul except an accidental attribute of it — namely, that it is a mover and a perceiver — and this is like whiteness for snow. What is sought is the genus of that which bears the accident, and it is not constitutive of the quiddity of the accident — I mean, substantiality is not constitutive of "mover" and "perceiver" in the way that essentials constitute. Likewise, whenever we have obtained only its image (khayāl) or its name, not its reality (ḥaqīqah), it is possible to seek the genus of that of which we have obtained the name or image. But in any other manner, this is not possible.

### Section: On Resolving a Sophism Concerning Circular Demonstration

If someone says: "Why have you judged circular demonstration (al-burhān al-dawrī) to be invalid? For it is known that when one inquires into causes and effects, according to what God has established as His custom in the interconnection of some of them with others, some of them return by circularity to the first — for it is said: 'Why was there a cloud?' And it is answered: 'Because there was vapor that condensed and congealed.' Then it is said: 'Why was there vapor?' And it is answered: 'Because the earth was moist, and heat acted upon it, so the parts of moisture evaporated and rose.' Then it is said: 'And why was the earth moist?' And it is answered: 'Because there had been rain.' Then it is said: 'And why was there rain?' And it is answered: 'Because there was a cloud.' So it returns by circularity to the cloud, as if it were said: 'Why was there a cloud?' and I answered: 'Because there was a cloud.' And the circular is invalid, whether the repeated term is separated by one intermediary or many, or not separated at all."

I say: This is not the invalid circularity. Rather, what is invalid is that a thing be taken in the explanation of itself identically — as when it is said: "Why was this very cloud?" and it is explained by what ultimately returns to explaining by this very cloud. As for returning to the explanation by another cloud, the cause is not identical in number to the effect, though it is equal to it in species. And there is no impossibility in one particular cloud being the cause of another cloud, through the intermediary of moistening the earth, then the rising of vapor, then its condensation into another cloud.

chapters.title_en: On What Constitutes True Demonstration (al-Burhān al-Ḥaqīqī)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فصل فيما يقوم فيه البرهان الحقيقي

إعلم أن البرهان الحقيقي ما يفيد اليقين الضروري الدائم الأبدي الذي
يستحيل تغييره كعلمك بان العالم حادث وأن له صانعا، وأمثال ذلك مما يستحيل
ان يكون بخلافه على الأبد، إذ يستحيل أن يحضرنا زمان نحكم فيه على العالم
بالقدم أوعلى الصانع بالنفي.
فأما الأشياء المتغيرة التي ليس فيها يقين دائم فهي جميع الجزئيات التي
في العالم الأرضي وأقربها إلى الثبات الجبال، وإذا قلت: هذا الجبل ارتفاعه
كذا، لم يكن الحاصل علما أبديا لأن المقدمة الصغرى ليس اليقين فيها دائما،
إذ ارتفاع الجبل يتصور تغيره، وكذا عمق البحار ومواضيع الجزائر، فهذه أمور
لا تبقى فكيف علمك يكون زيد في الدار. وأمثال ذلك مما يتعلق بالأحوال
الإنسانية العارضة لا كقولنا:
الإنسان حيوان والحيوان جسم والإنسان لا يكون في مكانين في حالة واحدة،
وأمثال ذلك فإن هذه يقينيات دائمية أبدية لا يتطرق إليها التغير حتى قال
بعض المتكلمين: العلم من جنس الجهل، وأراد به هذا الجنس من العلم. فإنك إذا
علمت بالتواتر مثلا أن زيدا في الدار، فلو فرض دوام هذا الإعتقاد في نفسك
وخروج زيد لكان هذا الإعتقاد بعينه قد صار جهلا، وهذاالجنس لا يتصور في
اليقينيات الدائمة. فإن قيل: هل يتصور إقامة البرهان على ما يكن وقوعه
أكثريا أو اتفاقيا؟ قلنا: أما الأكثري من الحدود الكبرى فلها لا محالة علل
اكثيرة، فتلك العلل إذا جعلت حدودا وسطى أفادت علما وظنا غالبا.
أما العلم فبكونه أكثريا غالبا فإنا إذا عرفنا من مجاري سنة الله  تعالى
أن اللحية إنما تخرج لاستحصاف البشرة ومتانة النجار، فإن عرفنا بكبر السن
استحصاف البشرة ومتانة النجار حكمنا بخروج اللحية أي حكمنا بأن الغالب
الخروج، وأن جهة الخروج غالبة على الجهة الأخرى، وهذا يقيني فإن ما يقع
غالبا فلمرجح لا محالة، ولكن بشرط خفي لا يطلع عليه، ويكون فوات ذلك الشرط
نادرا، ولذلك نحكم حكما يقينيا بأن من تزوج امرأة شابة ووطئها، فالغالب أن
يكون له ولد، ولكن وجود الولد بعينه مظنون وكون الوجود غالبا على الجملة
مقطوعبه، ولذلك نحكم في الفقهيات الظنية بأن العمل عند ظهور الظن واجب
قطعا، فيكون العمل مظنونا ووجود الحكم مظنونا، ولكن وجوب العمل قطعي
إذ علم بدليل قطعي إقامة الشرع غالب الظن مقام اليقين في حق وجوب العمل،
فكون الحكم مظنونا لم يمنعنا من القطع بما قطعنا به. وأما الأمور الإتفاقية
كعثور الإنسان في مشيه على كنز فمهما لا يمكن أن يحصل به ظن ولا علم، إذ لو
أمكن تحصل ظن بوجوده لصار غالبا أكثريا وخرج عن كونه إتفاقيا فقط.
نعم يمكن إقامة البرهان على كونه اتفاقيا فقط، وقد اصطلح المنطقيون على
تخصيص إسم البرهان بما ينتج اليقين الكلي الدايم الضروري، فإن لم تساعدهم
على هذا الإصطلاح أمكنك أن تسمي جميع العلوم الحقيقية برهانية إذا جمعت
المقدمات الشروط التي مضت، وأن ساعدتهم على هذا، فالبرهاني من العلوم العلم
بالله وصفاته وبجميع الأمور الأزلية التي لا تتغير كقولنا: الإثنان أكثر من
الواحد؛ فإن هذا صادق في الأزل، والأبد والعلم بهيئة السموات والكواكب
وإبعادها ومقاديرها وكيفية مسيرها يكون برهانيا عند من رأى أنها أزلية لا
تتغير، ولا تكون برهانية عند أهل الحق الذين يرون أن السموات كالأرضيات في
جواز تطرق التغير إليها.
وأما ما يختلف بالبقاع والأقطار كالعلوم اللغوية والسياسية إذ يختلف
بالإعصار والملل، وكالأوضاع الفقهية الشرعية من تفصيل الحلال والحرام فلا
يخفى أنها لا تكون من البرهانيات على هذا الإصطلاح. والفلاسفى يزعمون أن
السعادة الأخروية لا معنى لها إلا بلوغ النفس كمالها الذي يمكن أن  يكون
لها، وإن كمالها في العلوم لا في الشهوات،
ولما كانت النفس باقية أبدا كانت نجاتها وسعادتها في علوم صادقة أبدا
كالعلم بالله وصفاته وملائكته، وترتيب الموجودات وتسلسل الأسباب والمسببات.
فأما العلوم التي ليست يقينية دائمة فإن طلبت لم تطلب لذاتها، بل للتوصل
بها إلى غيرها، وهذا محل لا ينكشف إلا بنظر طويل، لا يحتمل هذا الكتاب
استقصاؤه بل محل بيانه العلوم المفصلة.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ر-ه-ن (burhān)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Clear, irrefutable proof; from root denoting whiteness and clarity — that which renders a matter luminous and decisive.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Demonstration yielding necessary, eternal certainty (yaqīn ḍarūrī) — the highest mode of apodictic evidence in the scale of knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense — a proof that is self-evidently decisive; metaphorical extension — any argument that silences opposition by its clarity.
- Root: ي-ق-ن (yaqīn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Certainty devoid of doubt; settled conviction that admits no perturbation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Firm knowledge (ʿilm) that excludes all possibility of error — the epistemic terminus of demonstration.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — unshakable assurance; metaphorical — applied to probable belief only by way of approximation, not true certainty.
- Root: غ-ل-ب (ghalabah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Predominance, overcoming; that which prevails over its opposite.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The customary prevailing (ghālib) in natural and legal matters — distinct from the universal and necessary.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — victory or preponderance; metaphorical — the frequent occurrence of an event over its contrary.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — governing the logical articulation of hypothetical cases (law, idhā) and exceptions (illā), as deployed in the author's dialectical objections and replies.
chapters.translation:
Know that true demonstration (al-burhān al-ḥaqīqī) is that which yields necessary, perpetual, eternal certainty (al-yaqīn al-ḍarūrī al-dāʾim al-abadī) whose alteration is impossible — such as your knowledge that the world is originated (ḥādith) and that it has a Maker, and similar matters of which it is impossible that they be otherwise for all eternity. For it is impossible that a time should come upon us in which we judge the world to be eternal (qadīm) or the Maker to be non-existent.

As for changing things in which there is no perpetual certainty — these are all the particulars (juzʾiyyāt) in the terrestrial world, the most stable of which are mountains. When you say, "This mountain has such-and-such a height," what results is not eternal knowledge, because the minor premise does not possess perpetual certainty therein — for the height of a mountain is conceivable to change. Likewise the depths of seas and the locations of islands — these are things that do not endure. How then [could your knowledge be eternal] when you say, "Zayd is in the house," and similar matters pertaining to accidental human states? Not like our saying: "Man is an animal, the animal is a body, and man cannot be in two places at one time," and the like — for these are perpetual, eternal certainties to which change finds no access. Indeed, some theologians (mutakallimūn) have said: "Knowledge is of the same genus as ignorance," intending thereby this genus of knowledge. For if you know by mass transmission (tawātur), for example, that Zayd is in the house, then were this belief supposed to persist in your soul while Zayd departed, this very belief would have become ignorance. But this genus is inconceivable in the perpetual certainties.

If it is said: "Is it conceivable to establish demonstration concerning what occurs for the most part (aktharī) or by accident (ittifāqī)?" We say: As for the frequent [occurrences] among the major terms, they have of necessity frequent causes. When those causes are made middle terms, they yield knowledge and predominant opinion (ẓann ghālib). As for knowledge — it is [knowledge] of its being frequent and predominant. For when we know, from the customary courses of God Most High's {«سُنَّةِ اللهِ»} practice, that the beard emerges only due to the coarseness of the skin and the firmness of the temperament, then if we know by old age the coarseness of the skin and firmness of temperament, we judge the emergence of the beard — that is, we judge that emergence is predominant, and that the direction of emergence prevails over the other direction. And this is certain — for what occurs predominantly has of necessity a preponderating cause (murjīḥ), but with a hidden condition not perceived, the failure of which condition is rare. For this reason we judge with certain judgment that whoever marries a young woman and has intercourse with her, it is predominant that he will have a child — yet the very existence of the child is a matter of opinion (maẓnūn), while the existence [of offspring] being predominant in general is a matter of certainty (maqṭūʿ bihi). Likewise we judge in probable jurisprudential matters (al-fiqhiyyāt al-ẓanniyyah) that acting upon the appearance of predominant opinion is obligatory with certainty (wājib qaṭʿan). Thus the act is probable and the existence of the ruling is probable, but the obligation of acting is certain — since it is known by a certain proof that the Lawgiver (al-Sharʿ) has established predominant opinion in the station of certainty regarding the obligation of action. So the fact that the ruling is probable did not prevent us from being certain of what we are certain of.

As for accidental matters (al-umūr al-ittifāqiyyah) — like a man stumbling while walking upon a treasure — no opinion or knowledge can be obtained concerning them. For were opinion of its existence possible, it would become frequent and predominant, and would exit from being merely accidental. Yes, demonstration can be established concerning its being merely accidental.

The logicians have agreed upon restricting the name "demonstration" (burhān) to that which yields universal, perpetual, necessary certainty. If you do not assist them in this convention, you may call all true sciences demonstrative when the premises gather the conditions that have preceded. But if you do assist them in this, then the demonstrative among the sciences is knowledge of God, His attributes, and all eternal matters that do not change — like our saying: "Two is more than one," for this is true in eternity past and eternity future. And knowledge of the configuration of the heavens, the stars, their distances, magnitudes, and the manner of their motion is demonstrative for those who hold them to be eternal and unchanging; but it is not demonstrative for the people of truth (ahl al-ḥaqq) who hold that the heavens are like the earthly things in the possibility of change befalling them.

As for what varies by regions and climes — like the linguistic and political sciences, since they vary by eras and religious communities — and like the jurisprudential religious ordinances (al-awḍāʿ al-fiqhiyyah al-sharʿiyyah) detailing the lawful and unlawful — it is not hidden that these are not among demonstrative matters on this convention.

The philosophers claim that ultimate happiness (al-saʿādah al-ukhrāwiyyah) has no meaning other than the soul's attainment of the perfection possible for it, and that its perfection lies in sciences, not in appetites. And since the soul endures forever, its deliverance and happiness lie in true sciences that endure forever — like knowledge of God, His attributes, His angels, the ordering of existents, and the chain of causes and effects. As for sciences that are not certain and perpetual, if they are sought, they are not sought for their own sake, but for reaching something else through them. This is a station that is not disclosed except by lengthy reflection, which this book cannot exhaust — rather, its exposition belongs to the detailed sciences.

chapters.title_en: On the Divisions of the Cause (Aqsām al-ʿIllah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فصل في أقسام العلة

العلة تطلق على أربعة معاني: الأول ما منه بذاته الحركة وهو السبب في
وجود الشيء كالنجار للكرسي والأب للصبي. الثاني المادة وما لا بد من وجوده
لوجود الشيء مثل الخشب للكرسي ودم الطمث والنطفة للصبي. والثالث الصورة وهي
تمام كل شيء وقد تسمى علة صورية كصورة السرير من السرير وصورة البيت للبيت.
الرابع الغاية الباعثة أولا المطلوب وجودها آخرا كالكن للبيت والصلوح
للجلوس من السرير.
واعلم أن كل واحد من هذه يقع حدودا وسطى في البراهين إذ يمكن أن يذكر كل
واحد في جواب لم. أما مبدأ الحركة فمثاله من المعقولات أن يقال: لم حارب
الأمير فلانا؟ فيقال: لأنه نهب ولايته،
فالنهب مبدأ الحركة. ويقال: لم اقتل فلانا؟ فيقال: لانه أكرهه السلطان
عليه. ومثاله من الفقه أن يقال: لم قتل هذا الشخص؟ فيقال: لأنه زنى أوارتد،
فيكون الزنا مبدأ هذا الأمر وهو الذي تسميه الفقهاء في الأكثر سببا، وأما
المادة فمثالها من المعقول أني قال: لم يموت الإنسان؟ فتقول: لأنه مركب من
أمور متنافرة من الحرارة والرطوبة والبرودة واليبوسة المتنازعة المتنافرة.
ومثاله من الفقه أن يقال: لم انفسخ القراض والوكالة بالموت والإغماء؟
فتقول: لأنه عقد ضعيف جائز لا لزوم له، وهذه علة ماديةإذ يرد الفسخ على
العقد ورود الموت على الإنسان عند جريان سبب هومبدأ الأمر في الموت والفسخ
جميعا.
وأما الصورة فبها قوام الشيء إذ السرير سرير بصورته لا بخشبه، والإنسان
إنسان بصورته لا بجسمه، والأشياء هيآتها بالصور لا بالمواد، فلا يخفى كون
القوام بها فإنه إذا قيلك لم صارت هذه النطفة  إنسانا وهذا الخشب سريرا؟
فيقال: بحصول صورة الإنسانية وحصول صورة السريرية. وأما الغاية التي
لأجلها الشيء فمثالها من المعقول أن يقال: لم عرضت الأضراس؟ فيقال: لأنها
يراد بها الطحن. ولم قاتلوا الطبقة الفلانية؟ فيقال: ليسترقوهم. وفي الفقه
يقال: لم قتل الزاني والمرتد والقاتل؟ فيقال: للزجر عن الفواحش. وهذه العلل
الأربع تجتمع في كل ما له علة، وكذا في الأحكام الفقهية، والفقهاء ربما
سموا المادة محلا والفاعل الذي هو كالنجار والأب أهلا، والغاية حكما، فإذا
فرض النكاح فالزوج أهل والبضع محل والحل غاية وصيغة العقد كأنها الصورة،
وما لم تجتمع هذه الأمور لا يتم للنكاح وجود، ولذلك قيل: النكاح الذي لا
يفيد الحل لا وجود له، وكذا البيع الذي لا يفيد الملك فإن وجود الغاية لا
بد منه، وكونها معقولا باعثا شرط قبل الوجود،
وكونها موجودة بالفعل واجب بعد الوجود، ومهما قدر الفاعل والمادة موجودا
لم يلزم وجود الشيء في كل حال كالنجار والخشب والأب والنطفة والبايع
والمبيع، ومهما وجدت الغاية بالفعل لزم وجود الشيء كالحل في النكاح والصلوح
للإكتنان والجلوس في البيت، والشيء بهذه الجهات الأربع يختلف في هذا
المعنى، ثم كل واحدة من هذه العلل إما بعيدة كإسلام المرأة للزوج عند ملك
الزوج نصف الصداق، فإنه علة الصداق، والصداق هوالعلة القريبة للتسليم، وإما
بالقوة كالإسكار للخمر قبل الشرب، وإما بالفعل كما في حال الشرب، وإما خاصة
كالزنا للرجم، وإما عامة كالجناية للرجم أو العقوبة، وأما بالذات وهو
المسمى علة عند الفقهاء كالزنا للرجم، وإما بالعرض كالإحصان له وهو الذي
يسمى شرطا، فإن الرجم لا يجب إلا بالإحصان، وهي خصال كمال ولكن يعمل عمل
العلة عنده، كما لو أرسلت الدعامة من تحت السقف فنزل فيقال نزوله بعلة
الثقل، ولكن عند إشالة الدعامة فإن للهوى شرطا، وهو فراغ جهة الأسفل عن جسم
صلب لا ينخرق. وأمثلة هذا في المعقولات كثيرة، فلذلك اقتصرنا على الأمثلة
الفقهية، والمقصود أن المعلل في الفقه والمعقول إذا توجهت المطالبة عليه
بالعلة، ينبغي أن يذكر العلة الخاصة  القريبة التي بالفعل حتى تقطع المطالبة
بلم، وإلا فيكون الطلب قائما.

### | كتاب الحد

والنظر في هذا الكتاب يحصره فنان: الأول فيما يجري من الحد يجري القوانين
الكلية.
والثاني في الحدود المفصلة.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Repetition and recurrence; a cause (ʿillah) is that which recurs with the effect, necessitating it repeatedly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, the ʿillah is the ontological ground (muʿallil) that entails the existence of the effect (maʿlūl), whether in origination (ḥudūth) or in essential constitution (taqwīm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes the efficient cause; metaphorical (majāz) extension covers material, formal, and final causes, as in juristic parlance where "cause" is often narrowed to the efficient motive (bāʿith).
- Root: غ-ي-ر (gh-y-r) — for ghāyah (end/purpose)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Terminal point, ultimate aim; that toward which a thing tends and in which it culminates.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The final cause (al-ʿillah al-ghāʾiyyah) is that which is intended first in conception (fi al-taṣawwur) but attained last in existence (fi al-wujūd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: spatial or temporal endpoint; metaphorical: the purposive motive that initiates action.
- Root: ص-و-ر (ṣ-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Form, shape, image; the principle by which a thing is what it is in actuality.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The formal cause (al-ʿillah al-ṣūriyyah) is the quiddity (māhiyyah) that constitutes the essence, distinguishing it from mere matter (mādda).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: visible shape; metaphorical: intelligible essence (ṣūrah ʿaqliyyah) by which a thing is defined.
- Root: م-د-د (m-d-d) — for mādda (matter)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: That which is extended, spread, and underlies; the substrate receiving form.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The material cause is that without which the thing cannot exist, though it does not by itself suffice for existence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical substance; metaphorical: the receptive subject (maḥall) in juristic rulings.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When multiple causes are enumerated with "the first... the second...", each term is syntactically appositive to the preceding, requiring precise nominal parsing (rafʿ) as predicates of an implied mubtadaʾ, ensuring the reader tracks the fourfold division without ambiguity.
chapters.translation:
I say: The term "cause" (ʿillah) is applied to four meanings. The first is that from which the motion proceeds by itself (mā minhu bi-dhātihi al-ḥarakah), and it is the efficient cause of the existence of a thing — like the carpenter for the chair, and the father for the child. The second is the matter (mādda), namely that whose existence is indispensable for the existence of the thing — like wood for the chair, and menstrual blood and the sperm-drop for the child. The third is the form (ṣūrah), which is the perfection (tamām) of every thing; it may be called the formal cause (ʿillah ṣūriyyah) — like the form of the bed from the bed, and the form of the house for the house. The fourth is the end (ghāyah), which is the first thing that incites (al-bāʿith awwalan) and the last thing sought in existence (al-maṭlūb wujūduhā ākhiran) — like shelter (al-kann) for the house, and fitness for sitting (al-ṣulūḥ lil-julūs) for the bed.

Know that each one of these can serve as a middle term (ḥadd awsaṭ) in demonstrations (barāhīn), for each can be cited in answer to "why?" (lima). As for the principle of motion (mabdaʾ al-ḥarakah), an example from the intelligibles is when one says: "Why did the commander fight so-and-so?" It is said: "Because he plundered his province" — so the plundering is the principle of motion. And it is said: "Why was so-and-so killed?" It is said: "Because the sultan compelled him to it." An example from jurisprudence (fiqh): "Why was this person killed?" It is said: "Because he committed adultery (zanā) or apostasy (irtidād)" — so the adultery is the principle of this matter, and this is what the jurists most often call the "cause" (sabab). As for the matter (mādda), an example from the intelligibles is when one says: "Why does man die?" You reply: "Because he is composed of mutually antagonistic elements — heat, moisture, cold, and dryness — which are conflicting and repugnant." An example from jurisprudence: "Why is the contract of qirāḍ (partnership) and wakālah (agency) dissolved by death and unconsciousness?" You reply: "Because it is a weak, revocable contract (ʿaqd ḍaʿīf jāʾiz) having no binding force (luzūm)" — and this is a material cause (ʿillah mādiyyah), for dissolution (fasakh) befalls the contract just as death befalls man, when a cause runs that is the principle of the matter in both death and dissolution alike.

As for the form (ṣūrah), by it the subsistence (qiwām) of the thing is achieved — for the bed is a bed by its form, not by its wood; and man is man by his form, not by his body. Things are constituted by their forms, not by their matters. So it is not hidden that subsistence is by the form; for when it is said: "Why did this sperm-drop become a man, and this wood a bed?" It is said: "By the attainment of the form of humanity (ṣūrat al-insāniyyah) and the attainment of the form of bed-ness (ṣūrat al-sarīriyyah)." As for the end (ghāyah) for the sake of which the thing exists, an example from the intelligibles is when one says: "Why were the molars created?" It is said: "Because they are intended for grinding." And: "Why did they fight such-and-such a class of people?" It is said: "To enslave them." In jurisprudence: "Why are the adulterer, the apostate, and the murderer killed?" It is said: "As a deterrent (zajr) against abominations (fawāḥish)."

These four causes all converge in everything that has a cause, and likewise in juristic rulings (aḥkām fiqhiyyah). The jurists sometimes call the matter the "locus" (maḥall), the agent — which is like the carpenter and the father — the "competent person" (ahl), and the end the "ruling" (ḥukm). Thus, if marriage (nikāḥ) is posited, the husband is the competent person (ahl), the pudendum is the locus (maḥall), the licitness (ḥill) is the end (ghāyah), and the formula of contract (ṣīghat al-ʿaqd) is as if it were the form (ṣūrah). Unless these matters are all assembled, the existence of marriage is not perfected. For this reason it is said: "A marriage that does not yield licitness has no existence." Likewise, a sale that does not yield ownership (milk) — for the existence of the end is indispensable. Its being an intelligible inciter (maʿqūl bāʿith) is a condition (sharṭ) prior to existence; and its being actually existent (mawjūdah bi-al-fiʿl) is obligatory after existence. Whenever the agent and the matter are posited as existing, the existence of the thing does not necessarily follow in every case — like the carpenter and the wood, the father and the sperm-drop, the seller and the sold object. But whenever the end is actually realized, the existence of the thing necessarily follows — like licitness in marriage, and fitness for shelter and sitting in the house. The thing, by these four aspects, varies in this meaning.
